In connection therewith read the chapter "Brightness."

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
And if you say evil also proceeds from Him,
Yet what damage is that to His perfection?

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
To send that evil is one of His perfections.
I will give you an illustration, O arrogant one;

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
The heavenly Artist paints His pictures of two sorts,
Fair pictures and pictures the reverse of fair.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Joseph he painted fair and made him beautiful;
He also painted ugly pictures of demons and 'afrits.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Both sorts of pictures are of His workmanship,
They proceed not from His imperfection, but His skill,

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
That the perfection of His wisdom may be shown,
And the gainsayers of His art be put to shame.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Could He not paint ugly things He would lack art,
And therefore He creates Guebers as well as Moslems.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Thus, both infidelity and faith bear witness to Him,
Both alike bow down before His almighty sway.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
But know, the faithful worship Him willingly,
For they seek and aim at pleasing Him;

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
While Guebers worship Him unwillingly,
Their real aim and purpose being quite otherwise.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Evil itself is turned into good for the good.
The Prophet said to that sick man,

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
"Pray in this wise and allay your difficulties;
'Give us good in the house of our present world,

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
And give us good in the house of our next world.
Make our path pleasant as a garden,

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
And be Thou, O Holy One, our goal!'"
The faithful will say on the last day, "O King!

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Was not Hell on the route all of us traveled?
Did not faithful as well as infidels pass through it?

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Yet on our way we perceived not the smoke of the fire;
Nay, it seemed Paradise and the mansion of the blessed."

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Then the King will answer, "That green garden,
As it appeared to you on your passage through it,

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Was indeed Hell and the place of dread torment;
Yet for you it became a garden green with trees.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Since you have labored to make hellish lusts,
And the 'fire of pride that courts destruction,

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
To make these, I say, pure and clean,
And, to please God, have quenched those fires,

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
So that the fire of lust, that erst breathed flame,
Has become a holy garden and a guiding light,

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Since you have turned the fire of wrath to meekness,
And the darkness of ignorance to shining knowledge,

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Since you have turned the fire of greed into bounty,
And the vile thorns of malice into a rose-garden;

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Since you have quenched all these fires of your own
For my sake, so that those poisons are now pure sweets;

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Since you have made fiery lust as a verdant garden,
And have sowed therein the seed of fidelity,

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
So that nightingales of prayer and praise
Ever warble sweetly around this garden;

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Since you have responded to the call of God,
And have drawn water out of the hell of lust,

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
For this cause my hell also, for your behoof,
Becomes a verdant garden and yields leaves and fruit."

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
What is the recompense of well-doing, O son?
It is kindness and good treatment and rich requital.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Have ye not said, "We are victims,
Mere nothings before eternal Being?

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
If we are drunkards or madmen,
'Tis that Cup-bearer and that Cup which make us so.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
We bow down our heads before His edict and ordinance,
We stake precious life to gain His favor.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
While the thought of the Beloved fills our hearts,
All our work is to do Him service and spend life for Him.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Wherever He kindles His destructive torch,
Myriads of lovers' souls are burnt therewith.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
The lovers who dwell within the sanctuary
Are moths burnt with the torch of the Beloved's face."

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
O heart haste thither, for God will shine upon you,
And seem to you a sweet garden instead of a terror.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
He will infuse into your soul a new soul,
So as to fill you, like a goblet, with wine.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Take up your abode in His soul!
Take up your abode in heaven, O bright full moon!

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Like the heavenly Scribe, He will open your heart's book
That He may reveal mysteries unto you.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Abide with your Friend, since you have gone astray,
Strive to be a full moon; you are now a fragment thereof.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Wherefore this shrinking of the part from its whole?
Why this association with its foes?

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Behold Genus become Species in due course,
Behold secrets become manifest through his light!

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
So long as woman-like you swallow blandishments,
How, O wise man, can you get relief from false flatteries?

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
These flatteries and fair words and deceits (of lust)
You take, and swallow, just like women.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
But the reproaches and the blows of Darveshes
Are really better for you than the praises of sinners.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Take the light blows of Darveshes, not the honey of sinners,
And become, by the fortune of good, good yourself.

loc.section: Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story X. Bayazid and the Saint.
text:
Because from them the robe of good fortune is gained,
In the asylum of the spirit blood becomes life.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text: Mo'avia, the first of the Ommiad Khalifas, was one day lying asleep in his palace, when he was awakened by a strange man. Mo'avia asked him who he was, and he replied that he was Iblis. Mo'avia then asked him why he had awakened him, and lblis replied that the hour of prayer was come, and he feared Mo'avia would be late. Mo'avia answered, "Nay! it could never have been your intention to direct me in the right way. How can I trust a thief like you to guard my interests?" Iblis answered, "Remember that I was bred up as an angel of light, and that I cannot quite abandon my original occupation. You may travel to Rome or Cathay, but still you retain the love of your fatherland. I still retain my love of God, who fed me when I was young; nay, even though I revolted from Him, that was only from jealousy (of Adam), and jealousy proceeds from love, not from denial of God. I played a game of chess with God at His own desire, and though I was utterly checkmated and ruined, in my ruin I still experience God's blessings."

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text: Mo'avia answered, "What you say is not credible. Your words are like the decoy calls of a fowler, which resemble the voices of the birds, and so lure them to destruction. You have caused the destruction of hundreds of mortals, such as the people of Noah, the tribe of 'Ad, the family of Lot, Nimrod, Pharaoh, Abu Jahl, and so on."

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text: Iblis retorted, "You are mistaken if you suppose me to be the cause of all the evil you mention. I am not God, that I should be able to make good evil, or fair foul. Mercy and vengeance are twin divine attributes, and they generate the good and evil seen in all earthly things. I am, therefore, not to blame for the existence of evil, as I am only a mirror, which reflects the good and evil existing in the objects presented to it."

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text: Mo'avia then prayed to God to guard him against the sophistries of lblis, and again adjured lblis to cease his arguments and tell plainly the reason why he had awakened him. Iblis, instead of answering, continued to justify himself, saying how hard it was that men and women should blame him when they did anything wrong, instead of blaming their own evil lusts. Mo'avia, in reply, reproached him with concealing the truth, and ultimately brought him to confess that the true reason why he had awakened him was this, that if he had overslept himself, and so missed the hour of prayer, he would have felt deep sorrow and have heaved many sighs, and each of these sighs would, in the sight of God, have counted for as many as two hundred ordinary prayers.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text: The value of sighs.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
A certain man was going into the mosque,
Just as another was coming out.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
He inquired of him what had occurred to the meeting,
That the people were coming out of the mosque so soon.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
The other told him that the Prophet
Had concluded the public prayers and mysteries.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
"Whither go you," said he, "O foolish one,
Seeing the Prophet has already given the blessing?"

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
The first heaved a sigh, and its smoke ascended;
That sigh yielded a perfume of his heart's blood.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
The other, who came from the mosque, said to him,
"Give me that sigh, and take my prayers instead."

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
The first said, "I give it, and take your prayers."
The other took that sigh with a hundred thanks.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
He went his way with deep humility and contrition,
As a hawk who had ascended in the track of the falcon.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
That night, as ho lay asleep, he heard a voice from heaven,
"Thou hast bought the water of life and healing;

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
The worth of what thou hast chosen and possessed
Equals that of all the people's accepted prayers."

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text: To illustrate the treachery of wolves in sheep's clothing, - of Satans rebuking sin and preaching religion - an anecdote is told of a master of a house who caught a thief, but was induced to let him escape by the stratagem of the thief's confederate, who cried that he had got the real thief elsewhere. Apropos of the same theme, the poet next relates the story of "those who built a mosque for mischief," as recorded in the Koran. The tribe of Bani Ganim built a mosque, and invited the Prophet to dedicate it. The Prophet, however, discovered that their real motive was jealousy of the tribe of Bani Amru lbn Auf, and of the mosque at Kuba, near Medina, and a treacherous understanding with the Syrian monk Abu Amir, and therefore he refused their request, and ordered the mosque to be razed to the ground.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text: Wisdom the believer's lost camel.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
My people adopt my law without obeying it,
They take that coin without assaying it.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
The Koran's wisdom is like the "believer's lost camel,'
Every one is certain his camel is lost.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
You have lost your camel and seek it diligently;
Yet how will you find it if you know not your own?

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
What was lost? Was it a female camel that you lost?
It escaped from your hand, and you are in a maze.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
The caravan is come to be loaded,
Your camel is vanished from the midst of it.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
You run here and there, your mouth parched with heat;
The caravan moves on, and night approaches.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
Your goods lie on the ground in a dangerous road,
You hurry after your camel in all directions.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
You cry "O Moslems, who has seen a camel,
Which escaped from its stable this morning?

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
To him who shall give me news of my camel
I will give a reward of so many dirhems."

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
You go on seeking news of your camel from every one,
And every lewd fellow flatters you with a fresh rumor,

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
Saying, "I saw a camel; it went this way;
'Twas red, and it went towards this pasture."

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
Another says, "Its ear was cropped."
Another says, "Its cloth was embroidered."

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
Another that it had only one eye,
Another that it had lost its hair from mange.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
To gain the reward every base fellow
Mentions a hundred marks without any foundation.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text: All false doctrines contain an element of truth.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
Just so every one in matters of doctrine
Gives a different description of the hidden subject.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
A philosopher expounds it in one way,
And a critic at once refutes his propositions.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
A third censures both of them;
A fourth spends his life in traducing the others.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
Every one mentions indications of this road,
In order to create an impression that he has gone it.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
This truth and that truth cannot be all true,
And yet all of them are not entirely astray in error.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
Because error occurs not without some truth,
Fools buy base coins from their likeness to real coins.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
If there were no genuine coins current in the world,
How could coiners succeed in passing false coins?

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
If there were no truth, how could falsehood exist?
Falsehood derives its plausibility from truth.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
'Tis the desire of right that makes men buy wrong;
Let poison be mixed with sugar, and they eat it at once.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
If wheat were not valued as sweet and good for food,
The cheat who shows wheat and sells barley would make no profit!

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
Say not, then, that all these creeds are false,
The false ones ensnare hearts by the scent of truth.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
Say not that they are all erroneous fancies,
There is no fancy in the universe without some truth.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
Truth is the "night of power " hidden amongst other nights,
In order to try the spirit of every night.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
Not every night is that of power, O youth,
Nor yet is every night quite void of power.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
In the crowd of rag-wearers there is but one Faqir;
Search well and find out that true one.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
Tell the wary and discerning believer
To distinguish the king from the beggar.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
If there were no bad goods in the world,
Every fool might be a skilful merchant;

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
For then the hard art of judging goods would be easy.
If there were no faults, one man could judge as well as another.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
Again, if all were faulty, skill would be profitless.
If all wood were common, there would be no aloes.

loc.section: Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XI. Mo'avia and Iblis.
text:
He who accepts everything as true is a fool,
But he who says all is false is a knave.

loc.section: Story XII. The Four Hindustanis who censured one another.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XII. The Four Hindustanis who censured one another.
text: Story XII. The Four Hindustanis who censured one another.

loc.section: Story XII. The Four Hindustanis who censured one another.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XII. The Four Hindustanis who censured one another.
text: Four Hindustanis went to the mosque to say their prayers. Each one duly pronounced the Takbir, and was saying his prayers with great devotion, when the Mu'azzin happened to come in. One of them immediately called out, "O Mu'azzin, have you yet called to prayer? It is time to do so." Then the second said to the speaker, "Ah! you have spoken words unconnected with worship, and therefore, according to the Hadis, you have spoiled your prayers." Thereupon the third scolded the last speaker, saying, "O simpleton, why do you rebuke him? Rather rebuke yourself." Last of all, the fourth said, "God be praised that I have not fallen into the same ditch as my three companions." The moral is, not to find fault with others, but rather, according to the proverb, to be admonished by their bad example. Apropos of this proverb, a story is told of two prisoners captured by the tribe of Ghuz. The Ghuzians were about to put one of them to death, to frighten the other, and make him confess where the treasure was concealed, when the doomed man discovered their object, and said, "O noble sirs, kill my companion, and frighten me instead."

loc.section: Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.
text: Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.

loc.section: Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.
text: An old man complained to his physician that he suffered from headache. The physician replied, "That is caused by old age." The old man next complained of a defect in his sight, and the physician again told him that his malady was due to old age. The old man went on to say that he suffered from pain in the back, from dyspepsia, from shortness of breath, from nervous debility, from inability to walk, and so on; and the physician replied that each of these ailments was likewise caused by old age. The old man, losing patience, said, "O fool, know you not that God has ordained a remedy for every malady?" The physician answered, "This passion and choler are also symptoms of old age. Since all your members are weak, you have lost the power of self-control, and fly into a passion at every word."

loc.section: Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.
text: Bad principles always produce bad acts.

loc.section: Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.
text:
Fools laud and magnify the mosque,
While they strive to oppress holy men of heart.

loc.section: Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.
text:
But the former is mere form, the latter spirit and truth.
The only true mosque is that in the hearts of saints.

loc.section: Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.
text:
The mosque that is built in the hearts of the saints
Is the place of worship of all, for God dwells there.

loc.section: Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.
text:
So long as the hearts of the saints are not afflicted,
God never destroys the nation.

loc.section: Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.
text:
Our forefathers lifted their hands against the prophets;
Seeing their bodies, they took them for ordinary men.

loc.section: Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.
text:
In you also abide the morals of those men of old;
How can you avoid fearing that you will act like them?

loc.section: Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.
text:
The morals of those unthankful ones dwell in you,
Your urn will not always return unbroken from the well.

loc.section: Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XIII. The Old Man and the Physician.
text:
Seeing that all these bad symptoms are seen in you,
And that you are one with those men, how can you escape?

loc.section: Story XIV. The Arab Carrier and the Scholar.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XIV. The Arab Carrier and the Scholar.
text: Story XIV. The Arab Carrier and the Scholar.

loc.section: Story XIV. The Arab Carrier and the Scholar.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XIV. The Arab Carrier and the Scholar.
text: An Arab loaded his camel with two sacks, filling one with wheat and the second with sand, in order to balance the first. As he was proceeding on his way he met a certain tradition-monger, who questioned him about the contents of his sacks. On learning that one contained nothing but sand, he pointed out that the object might be attained much better by putting half the wheat in one sack and half in the other. On hearing this, the Arab was so struck by his sagacity that he conceived a great respect for him, and mounted him on his camel. Then he said, "As you possess such great wisdom. I presume that you are a king or a Vazir, or at least a very rich and powerful noble." The theologian, replied, "On the contrary. I am a very poor man; all the riches my learning has brought me are weariness and headaches, and I know not where to look for a loaf of bread." The Arab said, "In that case get, off my camel and go your way, and suffer me to go mine, for I see your learning brings ill luck." The moral of the story is the worthlessness of mere human knowledge, and its inferiority to the divine knowledge proceeding from inspiration. This thesis is further illustrated by an account of the mighty works which were done by the saint Ibrahim bin Adham, through the divine knowledge that God had given him. Ibrahim was originally prince of Balkh, but renounced his kingdom and became a saint. One day he was sitting by the shore mending his cloak, when one of his former subjects passed by and marvelled to see him engaged in such a, mean occupation. The saint at once, by inspired knowledge, read his thoughts, and thus corrected his false impressions. He took the needle with which he was mending, his cloak and cast it into the sea. Then with a loud voice he cried out, "O needle rise again from the midst of the sea and come back again into my hands." Without a moment's delay thousands of fishes rose to the surface of the sea, each bearing in its mouth a golden needle, and cried out, "O Shaikh, take these needles of God!" Ibrahim then turned to the noble, saying, "Is not the kingdom of the heart better than the contemptible earthly kingdom I formerly possessed? What you have just seen is a very trifling sign of my spiritual power as it were, a mere leaf plucked to show the beauty of a garden. You have now caught the scent of this garden, and it ought to attract your soul to the garden itself, for you must know that scents have great influence, e.g., the scent of Joseph's coat, which restored Jacob's sight, and the scents which were loved by the Prophet."

God Almighty spake in the ear of Shu'aib,

text:
Thou sayest the very reverse of the truth, O fool!
Wandering from the way and lost in the desert!

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
How many times do I smite thee, and thou knowest not?
Thou art bound in my chains from head to foot.

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

So thou art blind to mysteries.

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

If that smoke touched a new kettle,
It would show the smut, were it only as a grain of barley;

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
For everything is made manifest by its opposite,
In contrast with its whiteness that black shows foul.

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

But when the kettle is black, then afterwards
Who can see on it the impression of the smoke?

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

His face agrees in color with the smoke.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

But if a man of Rum does blacksmith's work,
His face becomes grimed by the smoke fumes;

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

Then he quickly perceives the impression of his fault,
So that he wails and cries 'O Allah!'

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
When he is stubborn and follows his evil practices,
He casts dust in the eyes of his discernment.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
He recks not of repentance, and, moreover, that sin
Becomes dear to his heart, so that he becomes without faith,

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

Old shame for sin and calling on God quit him,
Rust five layers deep settles on his mirror,

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
Rust spots begin to gnaw his iron,
The color in his jewel grows less and less.

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
When you write on white paper,
What is written is read at a glance;

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
But when you write on the face of a written page,
It is not plain, reading it is deceptive;

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
For that black is written on the top of other black,
Both the writings are illegible and senseless.

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
Or if, in the third place, you write on the page,
And then blacken it like an infidel's soul,

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
Then what remedy but the aid of the Remedier?
Despair is copper and sight its elixir.

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
Lay your despair before Him,
That you may escape from pain without medicine."

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
When Shu'aib spoke these aphorisms to him,
From that breath of the soul roses bloomed in his heart,

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
His soul heard the revelations of heaven;
He said, "If He has punished me, where is the sign of it?"

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
Shu'aib said, "O Lord, he repels my arguments,
He seeks for a sign of that punishment."

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
The Veiler of sins replied, "I will tell him no secrets,
Save only one, in order to try him.

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
One sign that I punish him is this,
That he observes obedience and fasting and prayer,

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
And devotions and almsgiving, and so on,
Yet never feels the least expansion of soul.

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
He performs the devotions and acts enjoined by law,
Yet derives not an atom of relish from them.

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
Outward devotion is sweet to him, spirit is not sweet,
Nuts in plenty, but no kernel in any of them.

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
Relish is needed for devotions to bear fruit,
Kernels are needed that seeds may yield trees.

loc.section: Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XV. The Man who boasted that God did not punish him for his sins, and Jethro's answer to him.
text:
How can seeds without kernels become trees?
Form without soul (life) is only a dream."

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text: In a certain convent there lived a Sufi whose conduct gave just offence to the brethren. They brought him before their Shaikh and thus accused him, "This Sufi has three very bad qualities; he babbles exceedingly like a bell, at his meals he eats more than twenty men and when he sleeps he is as one of the Seven Sleepers." The Shaikh then admonished him, insisting on the obligation of keeping to the golden mean; and reminding him that even the prophet Moses was once rebuked by Khizr for speaking to excess. But the delinquent excused himself on the grounds that the mean is relative, what is excess in one man being moderation in another, that he who is led by the spirit is no longer subject to the outward law, and that, the "inner voice," which rules such an one s conduct, is its own evidence.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text: The mean is relative.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
He said, "Though the path of the mean is wisdom,
Yet is this same mean also relative.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
The water which is insufficient for a camel
Is like an ocean to a mouse.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
Whoso has four loaves as his daily allowance,
Whether he eat two or three, he observes the mean.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
But if he eat all four he transgresses the mean,
A very slave to greed, and voracious as a duck.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
Whoso has an appetite for ten loaves,
Know, though he eat six, he observes the mean.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
If I have an appetite for fifty loaves,
While you can manage only six, we are not on a par.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
You are wearied with ten prostrations in prayer,
Whilst I can endure five hundred.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
Such an one goes barefoot to the Ka'ba,
Whilst another faints with going to the mosque."

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text: The ecstatic state which exalts the subject of it above law.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
"At times my state resembles a dream,
My dreaming seems to them infidelity.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
Know my eyes sleep, but my heart is awake;
My body, though torpid, is instinct with energy.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
The Prophet said, 'Mine eyes sleep,
But my heart is awake with the Lord of mankind.'

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
Your eyes are awake and your heart fast asleep,
My eyes are closed, and my heart at the 'open door.'

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
My heart has other five senses of its own;
These senses of my heart view the two worlds.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
Let not a weakling like you censure me,
What, seems night to you is broad day to me;

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
What seems a prison to you is a garden to me.
Busiest occupation is rest to me.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
Your feet are in the mire, to me, mire is rose,
What to you is funeral wailing is marriage drum to me.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
While I seem on earth, abiding with you in the house,
I ascend like Saturn to the seventh heaven.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
'Tis not I who companion with you, 'tis my shadow;
My exaltation transcends your thoughts,

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
Because I have transcended thought,
Yea, I have sped beyond reach of thought.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
I am lord of thought, not overlorded by thought,
As the builder is lord of the building.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
All creatures are enslaved to thought;
For this cause are they sad at heart and sorrowful.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
I send myself on an embassy to thought,
And, at will, spring back again from thought.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
I am as the bird of heaven and thought as the fly,
How can the fly lend a helping hand to me?

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
Whoso has in him a spark of the light of Omnipotence,
However much he eats, say ' Eat on;' 'tis lawful to him."

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
To the spiritual man the "inner voice" is its
own evidence, and needs no other proof.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
"If you are a true lover of my soul,
This truth-fraught saying of mine is no vain pretence,

'Though I talk half the night I am superior to you;'

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
These two assertions of mine will both seem true to you
The moment you recognize the voice of your kinsman.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
Superiority and kinsmanship are both mere assertions,
Yet both are recognized for truth by men of clear wit.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
The nearness of the voice proves to such an one
That the voice proceeds from a friend who is near.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
The sweetness of the kinsman's voice, too, O beloved,
Proves the veracity of that kinsman.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
But the uninspired fool who from ignorance
Cannot tell the voice of a stranger from a friend's,

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
To him the friend's saying seems a vain pretension,
His ignorance is the material cause of his disbelief.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
To the wise, whose hearts are enlightened,
The mere sound of that voice proves its truth."

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
"When you say to a thirsty man, 'Come quickly;
This is water in the cup, take and drink it,'

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
Does the thirsty man say, 'This is a vain pretension;
Go, remove yourself from me, O vain pretender,

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
Or proceed to give proofs and evidence
That this is generic water, and concrete water thereof'?

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
Or when a mother cries to her sucking babe,
'Come, O son, I am thy mother,'

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
Does the babe answer, 'O mother, show a proof
That I shall find comfort from taking thy milk'?

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
In the hearts of every sect that has a taste of the truth
The sight and the voice of prophets work miracles.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
When the prophets raise their cry to the outward ear,
The souls of each sect bow in devotion within;

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
Because never in this world hath the soul's ear
Heard from any man the like of that cry.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVI. The Gluttonous Sufi.
text:
That poor man in that strange sweet voice
Recognizes the voice of God, 'Verily I am nigh.'"

loc.section: Story XVII. The Tree of Life.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVII. The Tree of Life.
text: Story XVII. The Tree of Life.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Tree of Life.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVII. The Tree of Life.
text: The preceding story is followed by a short anecdote of the infants of the Virgin Mary and the mother of John the Baptist leaping in their mothers' wombs, and in reply to matter of fact cavillers and questioners of this anecdote, the poet says we must look at its spirit and essential basis rather than its outward form. This introduces the story of the tree of life. A certain wise man related that in Hindustan there was a tree of such wonderful virtue that whosoever ate of its fruit lived forever. Hearing this, a king deputed one of his courtiers to go in quest of it. The courtier accordingly proceeded to Hindustan, and traveled all over that country, inquiring of every one he met where this tree was to be found. Some of these persons professed their entire ignorance, others joked him, and others gave him false information; and, finally, he had to return to his country with his mission unaccomplished. He then, as a last resource, betook himself to the sage who had first spoken of the tree, and begged for further information about it, and the sage replied to him as follows:

loc.section: Story XVII. The Tree of Life.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVII. The Tree of Life.
text:
The Shaikh laughed, and said to him, "O friend,
This is the tree of knowledge, O knowing one;

loc.section: Story XVII. The Tree of Life.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVII. The Tree of Life.
text:
Very high, very fine, very expansive,
The very water of life from the circumfluent ocean.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Tree of Life.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVII. The Tree of Life.
text:
Thou hast run after form, O ill-informed one,
Wherefore thou lackest the fruit of the tree of substance.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Tree of Life.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVII. The Tree of Life.
text:
Sometimes it is named tree, sometimes sun,
Sometimes lake, and sometimes cloud.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Tree of Life.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVII. The Tree of Life.
text:
'Tis one, though it has thousands of manifestations;
Its least manifestation is eternal life!

loc.section: Story XVII. The Tree of Life.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVII. The Tree of Life.
text:
Though 'tis one, it has a thousand manifestations,
The names that fit that one are countless.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Tree of Life.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVII. The Tree of Life.
text:
That one is to thy personality a father,
In regard to another person He may be a son.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Tree of Life.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVII. The Tree of Life.
text:
In relation to another He may be wrath and vengeance,
In relation to another, mercy and goodness.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Tree of Life.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVII. The Tree of Life.
text:
He has thousands of names, yet is One,
Answering to all of His descriptions, yet indescribable.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Tree of Life.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVII. The Tree of Life.
text:
Every one who seeks names, if he is a man of credulity,
Like thee, remains hopeless and frustrated of his aim.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Tree of Life.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVII. The Tree of Life.
text:
Why cleavest thou to this mere name of tree,
So that thou art utterly balked and disappointed?

loc.section: Story XVII. The Tree of Life.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVII. The Tree of Life.
text:
Pass over names and look to qualities,
So that qualities may lead thee to essence!

loc.section: Story XVII. The Tree of Life.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVII. The Tree of Life.
text:
The differences of sects arise from His names;
When they pierce to His essence they find His peace!"

loc.section: Story XVII. The Tree of Life.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVII. The Tree of Life.
text: This story is followed by another anecdote illustrative of the same thesis that attending merely to names and outward forms, rather than to the spirit and essence of religion, leads men into error and delusion. Four persons, a Persian, an Arab, a Turk, and a Greek, were traveling together, and received a present of a dirhem. The Persian said he would buy "angur" with it, the Arab said he would buy "inab," while the Turk and the Greek were for buying "uzum" and "astaphil" (staphyle), respectively. Now all these words mean one and the same thing, viz. "grapes;" but, owing to their ignorance of each other's languages, they fancied they each wanted to buy something different, and accordingly a violent quarrel arose between them. At last a wise man who knew all their languages came up and explained to them that they were all wishing for one and the same thing.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
Although a domestic fowl may have taken thee,
Who art a duckling, under her wing and nurtured thee,

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
Thy mother was a duck of that ocean.
Thy nurse was earthy, and her wing dry land.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
The longing for the ocean which fills thy heart,
That natural longing of thy soul comes from thy mother.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
Thy longing for dry land comes to thee from thy nurse;
Quit thy nurse, for she will lead thee astray.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
Leave thy nurse on the dry land and push on,
Enter the ocean of real Being, like the ducks!

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
Though thy nurse may frighten thee away from water,
Do thou fear not, but haste on into the ocean!

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
Thou art a duck, and flourishest on land and water,
And dost not, like a domestic fowl, dig up the house.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
Thou art a king of "the sons of Adam honored by God," l
And settest foot alike on sea and land;

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
For impress on thy mind, "We have carried them by sea,"
Before the words, "We have carried them by land."

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
The angels go not on dry land,
And the animals know nothing of the sea;

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
Thou in body art an animal, in thy soul an angel;
Hence thou goest both upon earth and on heaven."

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
Hence to outward view "He is a man like you,"
While to his sharp-seeing heart "it hath been revealed."

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
His earthy form has fallen on earth,
His spirit revolving above highest heaven.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
O boy, we are all of us waterfowl,
The sea knows full well our language.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
Solomon is, as it were, that sea, and we as the birds;
In Solomon we hold our course to eternity.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
Along with Solomon plunge into the ocean,
Then, like David, the water will make us coats-of-mail.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
That Solomon is present to every one,
But negligence closes their eyes and bewitches them.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
Hence, through ignorance, sloth, and folly,
Though he stands hard by us, we are shut off from him.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
The noise of thunder makes the head of the thirsty ache;
When he knows not that it unlocks the blessed showers,

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
His eyes are fixed on the running stream,
Unwitting of the sweetness of the rain from heaven.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
He urges the steed of his desire towards the caused,
And perforce remains shut off from the Causer.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.

display: Masnavi, Book 2, Story XVIII. The Young Ducks who were brought up under a Hen.
text:
Whoso beholds the Causer face to face,
How can he set his heart on things caused on earth?

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text: A PARTY of travelers lost their way in a wilderness, and were well nigh famished with hunger. While they were considering what to do, a sage came up and condoled with them on their unfortunate plight. He told them that there were many young elephants in the adjacent woods, one of which would furnish them an ample meal, but at the same time he warned them that if they killed one, its parents would in all probability track them out and be revenged on them for killing their offspring. Shortly after the travelers saw a plump young elephant, and could not resist killing and eating it. One alone refrained. Then they lay down to rest; but no sooner were they fast asleep than a huge elephant made his appearance and proceeded to smell the breath of each one of the sleepers in turn. Those whom he perceived to have eaten of the young elephant's flesh he slew without mercy, sparing only the one who had been prudent enough to abstain.: God's care for His children.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
O son, the pious are God's children,
Absent or present He is informed of their state.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Deem Him not absent when they are endangered,
For He is jealous for their lives.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
He saith, "These saints are my children,
Though remote and alone and away from their Lord.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
For their trial they are orphans and wretched,
Yet in love I am ever holding communion with them.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Thou art backed by all my protection;
My children are, as it were, parts of me.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Verily these Darveshes of mine
Are thousands on thousands, and yet no more than One;

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
For if not, how did Moses with one magic staff
Turn the realm of Pharaoh upside down?

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
And if it were not so, how did Noah with one curse
Make East and West alike drowned in his flood?

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Nor could one prayer of eloquent Lot
Have razed their strong city against their will,

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Their mighty city, like to Paradise,
Became as a Tigris of black water; go, see its vestige!

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Towards Syria is this vestige and memorial,
Thou seest it in passing on the way to Jerusalem.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Thousands of God-fearing prophets
In every age hold divine chastisements in hand.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Should I tell of them my limits would be exceeded,
And not hearts only but very hills would bleed."

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Evil deeds give men's prayers an ill savour in Gods nostrils.
Thou art asleep, and the smell of that forbidden fruit

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Ascends to the azure skies,
Ascends along with thy foul breath,

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Till it overpowers heaven with stench;
Stench of pride, stench of lust, stench of greed.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text: All these stink like onions when a man speaks.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Though thou swearest, saying, "When have I eaten?
Have I not abstained from onions and garlic?"

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
The very breath of that oath tells tales,
As it strikes the nostrils of them that sit with thee.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
So too prayers are made invalid by such stenches,
That crooked heart is betrayed by its speech.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
The answer to that prayer is, "Be ye driven into hell,"
The staff of repulsion is the reward of all deceit.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
But, if thy speech be crooked and thy meaning straight,
Thy crookedness of words will be accepted of God.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
That faithful Bilal, when he called to prayer,
Would devoutly cry, "Come hither, come hither!"

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
At last men said, "O Prophet, this call is not right,
This is wrong; now, what is thy intention?

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
O Prophet, and O ambassador of the Almighty,
Provide another Mu'azzin of better talent.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
'Tis an error at the beginning of our divine worship
To utter the words, 'Come to the asylum!'"

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
The wrath of the Prophet boiled up, and he said
(Uttering one or two secrets from the fount of grace),

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
"O base ones, in God's sight the 'Ho!' of Bilal
Is better than a hundred 'Come hithers' and ejaculations.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Ah! excite not a tumult, lest I tell forth openly
Your secret thoughts from first to last.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
If ye keep not your breath sweet in prayer,
Go, desire a prayer from the Brethren of Purity!"

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
For this cause spake God to Moses,
At the time he was asking aid in prayer,

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
"O Moses! desire protection of me
With a mouth that thou hast not sinned withal."

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Moses answered, "I possess not such a mouth."
God said, "Call upon me with another mouth!

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Act so that all thy mouths
By night and by day may be raising prayers.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
When thou hast sinned with one mouth,
With thy other mouth cry, 'O Allah!'

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Or else cleanse thy own mouth,
And make thy spirit alert and quick.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Calling on God is pure, and when purity approaches,
Impurity arises and takes its departure.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Contraries flee away from contraries;
When day dawns night takes flight.

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
When the pure name (of God) enters the mouth,
Neither does impurity nor that impure mouth remain!"

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
The man whose calling "O Allah" was equivalent
to God's answering him, "Here am I".

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
That person one night was crying, "O Allah!"
That his mouth might be sweetened thereby,

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
And Satan said to him, "Be quiet, O austere one!
How long wilt thou babble, O man of many words?

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
No answer comes to thee from nigh the throne,
How long wilt thou cry 'Allah' with harsh face?"

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
That person was sad at heart and hung his head,
And then beheld Khizr present before him in a vision,

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Who said to him, "Ah! thou hast ceased to call on God,
Wherefore repentest thou of calling upon Him?"

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
The man said, "The answer 'Here am I' came not,
Wherefore I fear that I am repulsed from the door."

loc.section: Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story I. The Travelers who ate the Young Elephant.
text:
Khizr replied to him, "God has given me this command;

loc.section: Story II. The Villager who invited the Townsman to visit him.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story II. The Villager who invited the Townsman to visit him.
text: A certain villager paid a visit to the town, and there received hospitality from one of the townsmen. At his departure the villager was profuse of thanks, and pressed the townsman to come and see him in his village, and bring his family with him. The townsman hesitated long before accepting his invitation, having doubts as to his sincerity, and remembering the Hadis, "Caution consists in suspecting others." But after ten years' solicitation he at length yielded, and set off with his family to the village. On his arrival the villager shut the door in his face, saying that he did not know him, and the townsman had to pass five nights in the cold and rain. At last, exhausted with suffering, he implored the villager to give him shelter, promising to render service in return. The villager granted it on condition that he would protect his garden from the wolves. The townsman accepted this condition, and taking bow and arrows, proceeded to patrol the garden, but, owing to the rain and the darkness, and his own fears, ended by shooting the villager's pet ass in mistake for a wolf. The villager abused him roundly, saying that he himself would not have taken an ass for a wolf, even on the darkest night. The townsman replied, "If that be so, you are self-convicted of inhumanity, for you must have recognized me, your friend of ten years' standing, the moment I knocked at your door. As for me, I am ignorant of all but Allah, and, moreover, was unable to see in the darkness; and God has said, 'No criminality is imputed to the blind.'2 But your blindness in refusing to recognize me was willful, and your claims to humanity are thus proved to be false by the test to which you have been submitted."

loc.section: Story III. The Jackal who pretended to be a Peacock.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story III. The Jackal who pretended to be a Peacock.
text: A jackal fell into a dye-pit, and his skin was dyed of various colors. Proud of his splendid appearance, he returned to his companions, and desired them to address him as a peacock. But they proceeded to test his pretensions, saying, "Dost thou scream like a peacock, or strut about gardens as peacocks are wont to do?" And he was forced to admit that he did not, whereupon they rejected his pretensions. Another story, also on the subject of false pretenders, follows. A proud man who lacked food procured a skin full of fat, greased his beard and lips with it, and called on his friends to observe how luxuriously he had dined. But his belly was vexed at this, because it was hungry, and he was destroying his chance of being invited to dinner by his friends. So the belly cried to God, and a cat came and carried off the skin of fat, and so the man's false pretences were exposed. The poet takes occasion to point out that Pharaoh's pretensions to divinity exactly resembled the pretensions of this jackal, and adds that all such false pretenders may be detected by the mark noted in the Koran, "Ye shall know them by the strangeness of their speech." This recalls the story of Harut and Marut, two angels who were very severe on the frailties of mankind, and whom God sent down upon the earth to be tempted, with the result that they both succumbed to the charms of the daughters of men.

In the course of the story the following anecdote is narrated:

loc.section: Story IV. Moses and Pharaoh.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story IV. Moses and Pharaoh.
text: A snake-catcher, who was following his occupation in the mountains, discovered a large snake frozen by the cold, and, imagining it to be dead, he tied it up and took it to Baghdad. There all the idlers of the city flocked together to see it, and the snake, thawed by the warmth of the sun, recovered life, and immediately destroyed the spectators.

If you wish to keep that snake tied up

loc.section: Story IV. Moses and Pharaoh.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story IV. Moses and Pharaoh.
text:
But how can base men attain this wish?
It requires a Moses to slay serpents;

loc.section: Story IV. Moses and Pharaoh.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story IV. Moses and Pharaoh.
text:
And a hundred thousand men were slain by his serpent,
In dire confusion, according to his purpose.

loc.section: Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.
text: Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.

loc.section: Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.
text: Some Hindoos were exhibiting an elephant in a dark room, and many people collected to see it. But as the place was too dark to permit them to see the elephant, they all felt it with their hands, to gain an idea of what it was like. One felt its trunk, and declared that the beast resembled a water-pipe; another felt its ear, and said it must be a large fan; another its leg, and thought it must be a pillar; another felt its back, and declared the beast must be like a great throne. According to the part which each felt, he gave a different description of the animal. One, as it were, called it "Dal" and another "Alif."

loc.section: Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.
text:
Comparison of the sensual eye to the
hand of one that felt the elephant.

loc.section: Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.
text:
The eye of outward sense is as the palm of a hand,
The whole of the object is not grasped in the palm.

loc.section: Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.
text:
The sea itself is one thing, the foam another;
Neglect the foam, and regard the sea with your eyes.

loc.section: Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.
text:
Waves of foam rise from the sea night and day,
You look at the foam ripples and not the mighty sea.

loc.section: Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.
text:
We, like boats, are tossed hither and thither,
We are blind though we are on the bright ocean.

loc.section: Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.
text:
Ah! you who are asleep in the boat of the body,
You see the water; behold the Water of waters!

loc.section: Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.
text:
Under the water you see there is another Water moving it,
Within the spirit is a Spirit that calls it.

loc.section: Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.
text:
Where were Moses and Jesus when that Sun
Showered down water on the fields sown with corn?

loc.section: Story V. The Elephant in a Dark Room.
