display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVI. The Woman who lost all her infants.
text:
The infidels know the prophets,
As well as they doubtless know their own children;

loc.section: Story XVI. The Woman who lost all her infants.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVI. The Woman who lost all her infants.
text:
Yea, the infidels know them as well as their own sons,
By a hundred tokens and a hundred evidences,

loc.section: Story XVI. The Woman who lost all her infants.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVI. The Woman who lost all her infants.
text:
But from envy and malice conceal their knowledge,
And incline themselves to say, "We know them not."

loc.section: Story XVI. The Woman who lost all her infants.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVI. The Woman who lost all her infants.
text:
So when God says in one place "knows them,"
In another He says, "None knows them beside me."

loc.section: Story XVI. The Woman who lost all her infants.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVI. The Woman who lost all her infants.
text:
For in truth they are hid under God's overshadowing,
And none but God knows them by actual experience.

loc.section: Story XVI. The Woman who lost all her infants.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVI. The Woman who lost all her infants.
text:
Therefore take this declaration with its context,
Remembering how you know and do not know Noah.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text: The Prince of Bokhara had a Vakil who, through fear of punishment for an offence he had committed, ran away and remained concealed in Kuhistan and the desert for the space of ten years. At the end of that time, being unable to endure absence from his lord and his home any longer, he determined to return to Bokhara and throw himself at his lord's feet, and endure whatever punishment his lord might be pleased to inflict upon him. His friends did all they could to dissuade him, assuring him that the Prince's wrath was still hot against him, and that if he appeared at Bokhara he would be put to death, or at least imprisoned for the rest of his life. He replied, "O advisers, be silent, for the force of the love which is drawing me to Bokhara is stronger than the force of prudent counsels. When love pulls one way all the wisdom of Abu Hanifa and Ash-Shafi'i is impotent to withstand it. If it shall please my lord to slay me, I will yield up my life without reluctance, for this life of estrangement from him which I am now leading is the same as death, and release from it will be eternal happiness. I will return to Bokhara and throw myself at my lord's feet, and say to him, 'Deal with me as thou wilt, for I can no longer bear absence from thee, and life or death at thy hands is all the same to me!'" Accordingly, he journeyed back to Bokhara, counting the very toils and discomforts of the road sweet and delightful, because they were steps in his homeward course. When he reached Bokhara his friends and relations all warned him not to show himself, as the Prince was still mindful of his offence and bent on punishing him; but he replied to them as to his other advisers, that he was utterly regardless of his life, and was resolved to commit himself to his lord's good pleasure. He then went to the court and threw himself at his lord's feet and swooned away. The Prince, seeing the strong affection borne to him by his repentant servant, conceived a similar affection towards him, and descended from his throne and graciously raised him from the ground, and pardoned his offence. Thus it is that eternal life is gained by utter abandonment of one's own life. When God appears to His ardent lover the lover is absorbed in Him, and not so much as a hair of the lover remains. True lovers are as shadows, and when the sun shines in glory the shadows vanish away. He is a true lover of God to whom God says, "I am thine, and thou art mine!"

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text: In the course of this story, which is narrated at great length, are introduced anecdotes of a lover and his mistress, of the Virgin Mary being visited by the "Blessed Spirit" or Angel Gabriel, of the fatal mosque, of Galen's devotion to carnal learning, of Satan's treachery to the men of Mecca at the battle of Bedr, and of Solomon and the gnat. There also occur comments on various texts, and a curious comparison of the trials and wholesome afflictions of the righteous to the boiling of potherbs in a saucepan by the cook.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text: The reply of the lover when asked by his mistress which city of all those he had seen was most pleasing in his sight.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
A damsel said to her lover, "O fond youth,
You have visited many cities in your travels;

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Which of those cities seems most delightful to you?"
He made answer, "The city wherein my love dwells.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
In whatever nook my queen alights,
Though it be as the eye of a needle, 'tis a wide plain;

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Wherever her Yusuf-like face shines as a moon,
Though it be the bottom of a well, 'tis Paradise.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
With thee, my love, hell itself were heaven,
With thee a prison would be a rose-garden.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
With thee hell would be a mansion of delight,
Without thee lilies and roses would be as flames of fire!"

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text: The answer of the Vakil to those who advised him not to court death by yielding himself up to his lord.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
He said, "I am a drawer of water; water attracts me,
Even though I know water may be my death.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
No drawer of water flees from water,
Even though it may cause him a hundred deaths.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Though it may make my hand and belly dropsical,
My love for water will never be lessened.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
I should say, when they asked me about my belly,
'Would that the ocean might flow into it!'

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Though the bottle of my belly were burst with water,
And though I should die, my death would be acceptable.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Wheresoever I see one seeking water, I envy him,
And cry, 'Would I were in his place!'

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
My hand is a tabor and my belly a drum,
Like the rose I beat the drum of love of water.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Like the earth or like a fetus I devour blood,
Since I became a lover this is my occupation.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
If that 'Faithful Spirit' should shed my blood,
I would drink it up drop by drop like the earth.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
At night I boil on the fire like a cooking-pot,
From morn till eve I drink blood like the sand.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
It repents me that I planned a stratagem,
And that I fled from before his wrath.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Tell him to sate his wrath on my poor life,
He is the 'Feast of Sacrifice,' and I his loving cow.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The cow, whether it eats or sleeps,
Thinks of naught but sacrificing itself.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Know me to be that cow of Moses which gave its life,
Each part of me gives life to the righteous.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
That cow of Moses was made a sacrifice,
And its least part became a source of life.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
That murdered man leapt up from his deadness
At the words, ' Strike the corpse with part of her.'

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
O pious ones, slay the cow (of lust),
If ye desire true life of soul and spirit!

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
I died as inanimate matter and arose a plant,
I died as a plant and rose again an animal.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
I died as an animal and arose a man.
Why then should I fear to become less by dying?

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
I shall die once again as a man
To rise an angel perfect from head to foot!

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Again when I suffer dissolution as an angel,
I shall become what passes the conception of man!

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Let me then become non-existent, for non-existence
Sings to me in organ tones, 'To him shall we return.'

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Know death to be the gathering together of the people.
The water of life is hidden in the land of darkness.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Like a water-lily seek life there!
Yea, like that drawer of water, at the risk of life,

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Water will be his death, yet he still seeks water,
And still drinks on, and God knows what is right.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
O lover, cold-hearted and void of loyalty,
Who from fear for your life shun the beloved!

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
O base one, behold a hundred thousand souls
Dancing towards the deadly sword of his love:

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Behold water in a pitcher; pour it out;
Will that water run away from the stream?

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
When that water joins the water of the stream
It is lost therein, and becomes itself the stream.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Its individuality is lost, but its essence remains,
And hereby it becomes not less nor inferior.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
I will hang myself upon my lord's palm-tree
In excuse for having fled away from him!"

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Even as a ball rolling along on head and face,
He fell at the feet of the Prince with streaming eyes.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The people were all on the alert, expecting
That the Prince would burn him or hang him,

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Saying, "Moth-like he has seen the blaze of the light,
And fool-like has plunged therein and lost his life."

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
But the torch of love is not like that torch,
'Tis light, light in the midst of light,

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
'Tis the reverse of torches of fire,
It appears to be fire, but is all sweetness.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Love generates love. "If ye love God, God will love you"
That. Bokharian then cast himself into the flame,

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
But his love made the pain endurable;
And as his burning sighs ascended to heaven,

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The love of the Prince was kindled towards him.
The heart of man is like the root of a tree,

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Therefrom grow the leaves on firm branches.
Corresponding to that root grow up branches

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text: As well on the tree as on souls and intellects.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The tops of the perfect trees reach the heavens,
The roots firm, and the branches in the sky.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Since then the tree of love has grown up to heaven,
How shall it not also grow in the heart of the Prince?

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
A wave washes away the remembrance of the sin from his heart,
For from each heart is a window to other hearts.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Since in each heart there is a window to other hearts,
They are not, separated and shut off like two bodies.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Thus, even though two lamp-dishes be not joined,
Yet their light is united in a single ray.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
No lover ever seeks union with his beloved,
But his beloved is also seeking union with him.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
But the lover's love makes his body lean,
While the beloved's love makes hers fair and lusty.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
When in this heart the lightning spark of love arises,
Be sure this love is reciprocated in that heart.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
When the love of God arises in thy heart,
Without doubt God also feels love for thee.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The noise of clapping of hands is never heard
From one of thy hands unaided by the other hand

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The man athirst cries, "Where is delicious water?"
Water too cries, "Where is the water-drinker?"

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
This thirst in my soul is the attraction of the water;
I am the water's and the water is mine.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
God's wisdom in His eternal foreknowledge and decree
Made us to be lovers one of the other.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Nay more, all the parts of the world by this decree
Are arranged in pairs, and each loves its mate.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Every part of the world desires its mate,
Just as amber attracts blades of straw.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Heaven says to earth, "All hail to thee!
We are related to one another as iron and magnet."

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Heaven is man and earth woman in character;
Whatever heaven sends it, earth cherishes.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
When earth lacks heat, heaven sends heat;
When it lacks moisture and dew, heaven sends them.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The earthy sign succours the terrestrial earth,
The watery sign (Aquarius) sends moisture to it;

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The windy sign sends the clouds to it,
To draw off unwholesome exhalations.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The fiery sign (Leo) sends forth the heat of the sun,
Like a dish heated red-hot in front and behind.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The heaven is busily toiling through ages,
Just as men labor to provide food for women.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
And the earth does the woman's work, and toils
In bearing offspring and suckling them.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Know then earth and heaven are endued with sense,
Since they act like persons endued with sense.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
If these two lovers did not suck nutriment from each other,
Why should they creep together like man and wife?

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Without the earth how could roses and saffron grow?
For naught can grow from the sole heat and rain of heaven.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
This is the cause of the female seeking the male,
That the work of each may be accomplished.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
God has instilled mutual love into man and woman,
That the world may be perpetuated by their union.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Earth says to the earth of the body, "Come away,
Quit the soul and come to me as dust.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Thou art of my genus, and wilt be better with me,
'Thou had'st better quit the soul and fly to me!"

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Body replies "True, but my feet are fast bound,
Though like thee I suffer from separation."

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Water calls out to the moisture of the body,
"O moisture, return to me from your foreign abode!"

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Fire also calls out to the heat of the body,
"Thou art of fire; return to thy root!"

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
In the body there are seventy-and-two diseases;
It is ill compacted owing to the struggle of its elements.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Disease comes to rend the body asunder,
And to drag apart its constituent elements.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The four elements are as birds tied together by the feet;
Death, sickness and disease loose their feet asunder.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The moment their feet are loosed from the others,
'The bird of each element flies off by itself.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The repulsion of each of these principles and causes
Inflicts every moment a fresh pang on our bodies.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
That it may dissolve these composite bodies of ours,
The bird of each part tries to fly away to its origin;

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
But the wisdom of God prevents this speedy end,
And preserves their union till the appointed day.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
He says, "O parts, the appointed time is not yet;
It is useless for you to take wing before that day."

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
But as each part desires reunion with its original,
How is it with the soul who is a stranger in exile?

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
It says, "O parts of my habitation here below,
My absence is sadder than yours, as I am heaven-born.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The body loves green pastures and running water,
For this cause that its origin is from them.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The love of the soul is for life and the living one,
Because its origin is the Soul not bound to place.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The love of the soul is for wisdom and knowledge,
That of the body for houses, gardens, and vineyards;

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The love of the soul is for things exalted on high,
That of the body for acquisition of goods and food.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The love too of Him on high is directed to the soul:
Know this for 'He loves them that love Him.'"

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The sum is this, that whoso seeks another,
The soul of that other who is sought inclines to him.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Let us quit the subject. Love for that soul athirst
Was kindled in the breast of the Prince of Bokhara.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The smoke of that love and the grief of that burning heart
Ascended to his master and excited his compassion.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text: The praises addressed to the Prince by the Vakil.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
He said, "O phoenix of God and goal of the spirit
I thank thee that thou hast come back from Mount Qaf!

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
O Israfil of the resurrection-day of love,
O love, love, and heart's desire of love!

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Let thy first boon to me be this,
To lend thine ear to my orisons.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Though thou knowest my condition clearly,
O protector of slaves, listen to my speech.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
A thousand times, O prince incomparable,
Has my reason taken flight in desire to see thee,

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
And to hear thee and to listen to thy words,
And to behold thy life-giving smiles.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Thy inclining thine ear to my supplications
Is as a caress to my misguided soul.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The baseness of my heart's coin is known to thee,
But thou hast accepted it as genuine coin.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Thou art proud towards the arrogant and proud;
All clemencies are as naught to thy clemency.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
First hear this, that while I remained in absence,
First and last alike escaped me.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Secondly, hear this. O prince beloved,
That I searched much, but found no second to thee.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Thirdly, that when I had departed outside thee,
I said it was like the Christian Trinity.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Fourthly, when my harvest was burned up,
I knew not the fourth from the fifth.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Wheresoever thou findest blood on the roads,
Trace it, and 'tis tears of blood from my eyes.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
My words are thunder, and these sighs and tears
Are drawn by it as rain from the clouds.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
I am distracted between speaking and weeping.
Shall I weep, or shall I speak, or what shall I do?

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
If I speak, my weeping ceases;
If I weep, I cease to praise and magnify thee."

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
He spoke thus, and then fell to weeping,
So that high and low wept with him.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
So many "Ahs" and "Alases" proceeded from his heart,
That the people of Bokhara formed a circle round him.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Talking sadly, weeping sadly, smiling sadly,
Men and women, small and great, were all assembled.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
The whole city wept in concert with him;
Men and women mingled together as on the last day.

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Then Heaven said to Earth,
"If you never saw a resurrection-day, see it here!"

loc.section: Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVII. The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara.
text:
Reason was amazed, saying, "What love, what ecstasy!
Is his separation more wondrous, or his reunion?"

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text: In the suburbs of a certain city there was a mosque in which none could sleep a night and live. Some said it was haunted by malevolent fairies; others, that it was under the baneful influence of a magic spell; some proposed to put up a notice warning people not to sleep there, and others advised that the door should be kept locked. At last a stranger came to that city and desired to sleep in the mosque, saying that he did not fear to risk his life, as the life of the body was naught, and God has said, "Wish for death if you are sincere." The men of the city warned him again and again of the danger, and rebuked him for his foolhardiness, reminding him that not improbably Satan was tempting him to his own destruction, as he tempted the men of Mecca at the battle of Bedr. The stranger, however, would not be dissuaded, but persisted in his purpose of sleeping in the mosque. He said that he was as one of the devoted agents of the Ismailians, who were always ready to sacrifice their lives at the bidding of their chiefs, and that the terrors of death did not appal him any more than the noise of a little drum beaten by a boy to scare away birds could appal the great drum-bearing camel that used to march at the head of King Mahmud's army. Accordingly, he slept in the mosque, and at midnight he was awakened by a terrible voice, as of one about to attack him. But instead of being dismayed, he bethought himself of the text "Assault them with thy horsemen and thy footmen," and confronted his unseen foe, challenging him to show himself and stand to his arms. At these words the spell was dissipated, and showers of gold fell on all sides, which the brave hero proceeded to appropriate.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text: The "knowledge of certainty" and the "eye of certainty".

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Our body and substance are snow, doomed to perish,
God is He who buys them, for "God hath bought them."

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
You prefer this perishing snow to God's price
Because you are in doubt and have not certainty;

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
And, strange to say, opinion abides in you, O weak one,
And never flies away to the garden of certainty.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Every opinion is aiming at certainty, O son,
And more and more moves its wings towards certainty.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
When it reaches knowledge it stands erect,
And its knowledge again hastes on towards certainty,

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Because in the approved road of the faith
Knowledge is lower than certainty, but above opinion.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Know knowledge aspires to certainty,
And certainty again to sight and ocular evidence.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
In the chapter, "Desire of riches occupieth you,"
After "Nay," read "Would that ye knew!"

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Knowledge conducts you to sight, O knower!
"If ye are certain, ye shall see hell-fire."

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Sight follows on certainty with no interval,
Just as reasoned knowledge is born of opinion.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
See the account of this in the chapter cited,
How knowledge of certainty becomes the eye of certainty.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
As for me, I am above both opinion and certainty;
My head is not affected by your cavils.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Since my mouth has eaten of His sweetmeats,
I am become clear-sighted, and see him face to face!

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text: The righteous are exposed to trials for their improvement, as potherbs are boiled to make them fit for food.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Behold these potherbs boiling in the pot,
How they jump and toss about in the heat of the fire.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Whilst they are boiling, they keep leaping up,
Even to the top of the pot, and utter cries,

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Saying to the housewife, "Why do you set us on the fire?
Now you have bought us, why should you afflict us?"

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
The housewife pushes them down with her spoon, saying,
"Be still, and boil well, and leap not off the fire.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
I do not boil you because I dislike you,
But that you may acquire a good savor and taste.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
When you become food you will be mingled with life;
This trial is not imposed on you to distress you.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
In the garden you drank water soft and fresh;
That water-fed one was reserved for this fire.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Mercy was first shown to it before vengeance,
That mercy might train it to be proof against trial;

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Mercy was shown to it previously to vengeance,
That it might acquire its substance of being.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Because flesh and skin grow not without tender care,
How should they not grow when warmed by the Friend's love.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
If vengeance follows as a necessary consequence,
That you may make an offering of that substance,

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Mercy follows again to compensate for it,
That you may be purified and raised above your nature.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
I am Abraham, and you his son under the knife.
Lay down your head! 'I have seen I must sacrifice you.'

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Yield your head to vengeance, your heart to constancy,
That I may cut your throat like an Ismailian's.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
I cut off your head, but that head is such
That it is restored to life by being cut off!"

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
My main object herein is to inculcate resignation,
O Mosalman! it behoves you to seek resignation.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
O potherbs, you boil in trials and sufferings
That neither existence nor self may remain in you.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Though you once smiled in that earthly garden,
You are really roses of the garden of life and sight.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
If you are torn away from the garden of earth,
You become sweet food to revive man's life;

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Yea, become his food and strength and thought!
You were only milk, you become a lion of the forest!

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
You issue from God's attributes at first;
Return again back to those attributes with all speed!

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
You come from the clouds and sunshine and sky,
Then assume moral qualities and ascend the sky.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
You come in the form of rain and sunshine,
You depart endued with excellent attributes.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
You begin as a part of the sun, clouds, and stars,
You rise to be breath, act, word, and thought!

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
The life of animals comes from the death of plants.
True is the saying, 'Kill me, O faithful ones!'

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Since such exaltation awaits us after death.
True it is that 'In our death is life.'

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Acts, words, and faith are the food of the King,
So that in this ascent one attains to heaven.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Thus, as potherbs become the food of men,
They rise above the grade of minerals to that of animals.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text: Objections of fools to the Masnavi.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
A certain goose pops his head out of his coop,
And displays himself as a critic of the Masnavi,

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Saying, "This poem, the Masnavi, is childish;
'Tis but a story of the prophets, and so on.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
'Tis not an account of the arguments and deep mysteries,
Whereto holy men direct their attention;

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Concerning asceticism, and so on to self-annihilation,
Step by step, up to communion with God;

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
An explanation and definition of each several state,
Whereto the men of heart ascend in their flight."

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Whereas the Book of God resembles the Masnavi in this,
The infidels abused it, in the same manner,

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Saying, 'It contains old tales and stories;
There is no deep analysis or lofty investigation therein.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Little boys can understand it;
It only contains commands and prohibitions,

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Accounts of Yusuf and his curled locks,
Accounts of Jacob, of Zulaikha and her love,

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Accounts of Adam, of the wheat, and of the serpent Iblis,
Accounts of Hud, of Noah, of Abraham, and the, fire."

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Know the words of the Koran are simple,
But within the outward sense is an inner secret one.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Beneath that secret meaning is a third,
Whereat the highest wit is dumbfoundered.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
The fourth meaning has been seen by none
Save God, the Incomparable and All-sufficient.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Thus they go on, even to seven meanings, one by one,
According to the saying of the Prophet, without doubt.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Do thou, O son, confine not thy view to the outward meaning,
Even as the demons saw in Adam only clay.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
The outward meaning of the Koran is like Adam's body,
For its semblance is visible, but its soul is hidden.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
O reviling dog! thou makest a clamour,
Thou makest thy abuse of the Koran thy destruction.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
This is not a lion, wherefrom thou canst save thy life,
Or canst secure thyself from his talons!

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
The Koran cries out even to the last day,
"O people, given up as a prey to ignorance,

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
If ye have imagined me to be only empty fables,
Ye have sown the seed of reviling and infidelity.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Ye yourselves who abuse me will see yourselves
Annihilated, and made like a tale that is told!"

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text: Solomon and the gnat.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
A gnat came in from the garden and fields,
And called on Solomon for justice,

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Saying, "O Solomon, you extend your equity
Over demons and the sons of Adam and fairies.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Fish and fowl dwell under the shelter of your justice;
Where is the oppressed one whom your mercy has not sought?

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Grant me redress, for I am much afflicted,
Being cut off from my garden and meadow haunts."

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Then Solomon replied, "O seeker of redress,
Tell me from whom do you desire redress?

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Who is the oppressor, who, puffed up with arrogance
Has oppressed you and smitten your face?"

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
The gnat replied, "He from whom I seek redress is the Wind,
'Tis he who has emitted the smoke of oppression at me;

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Through his oppression I am in a grievous strait,
Through him I drink blood with parched lip!"

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Solomon replied to him, "O sweet voiced one,
You must hear the command of God with all your heart.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
God has commanded me saying, 'O dispenser of justice,
Never hear one party without the other!'

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Till both parties come into the presence,
The truth is never made plain to the judge."

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
When the Wind heard the summons, it came swiftly,
And the gnat instantly took flight.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
In like manner the seekers of God's presence-seat,
When God appears, those seekers vanish.

loc.section: Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.

display: Masnavi, Book 3, Story XVIII. The Deadly Mosque.
text:
Though that union is life eternal,
Yet at first that life is annihilation.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text: THE fourth book begins with an address to Husamu-'d-Din, and this is followed by the story of the lover and his mistress, already commenced in the third book. A certain lover had been separated from his mistress for the space of seven years, during which he never relaxed his efforts to find her. At last his constancy and perseverance were rewarded, in accordance with the promises "The seeker shall find," and "Whoso shall have wrought an atom's weight of good shall behold it." One night, as he was wandering through the city, he was pursued by the patrol, and, in order to escape them, took refuge in a garden, where he found his long-sought mistress. This occasioned him to reflect how often men "hate the things that are good for them," and led him to bless the rough patrol who had procured him the bliss of meeting with his mistress.: Apropos of this, an anecdote is told of a preacher who was in the habit of blessing robbers and oppressors, because their evil example had turned him to righteousness. The moment the lover found himself alone with his mistress, he attempted to embrace her, but his mistress repulsed him, saying, that though no men 'were present, yet the wind was blowing and that showed that God, the mover of the wind, was also present. The lover replied, "It may be I am lacking in good manners, but I am not lacking in constancy and fidelity towards you." His mistress replied, "One must judge of the hidden by the manifest; I see for myself that your outward behavior is bad, and thence I cannot but infer that your boast of hidden virtues is not warranted by actual facts. You are ashamed to misconduct yourself in the sight of men, but have no scruple to do so in the presence of the All-seeing God, and hence I doubt the existence of the virtuous sentiments which you claim to possess, but which can only be known to yourself." To illustrate this, she told the story of a Sufi and his faithless wife. This wife was one day entertaining a paramour, when she was surprised by the sudden return of her husband. On the spur of the moment she threw a woman's dress over her paramour and presented him to her husband as a rich lady who had come to propose a marriage between her son and the Sufi's daughter, saying she did not care for wealth, but only regarded modesty and rectitude of conduct. To this the Sufi replied, that as from her coming unattended it was plain that the lady had not the wealth she pretended to have, it was more than probable that her pretensions to extraordinary modesty and humility were also fictitious. The lover then proceeded to excuse himself by the plea that he had wished to test his mistress, and ascertain for himself whether she was a modest woman or not. He said he of course knew beforehand that she would prove to be a modest woman, but still he wished to have ocular demonstration of the fact. His mistress reproved him for trying to deceive her with false pretences, assuring him that, after he had been detected in a fault, his only proper course was to confess it, as Adam had done. Moreover, she added that an attempt to put her to the test would have been an extremely unworthy proceeding, only to be paralleled by Abu Jahl's attempt to prove the truth of the Prophet's claims by calling on him to perform a miracle.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text: The soul of good in things evil. Evil only relative.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
The lover invoked blessings on that rough patrol,
Because their harshness had wrought bliss for him.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
They were poison to most men, but sweets to him,
Because those harsh ones had united him with his love.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
In the world there is nothing absolutely bad;
Know, moreover, evil is only relative.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
In the world there is neither poison nor antidote,
Which is not a foot to one and a fetter to another;

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
To one the power of moving, to another a clog;
To one a poison, to another an antidote.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Serpents' poison is life to serpents,
In relation to mankind it is death.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
To the creatures of the sea the sea is a garden,
To the creatures of the land it is fatal.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
In the same way, O man, reckon up with intelligence
The relations of these things in endless variety.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
In relation to this man Zaid is as Satan,
In relation to another he is as a Sultan.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
The latter calls Zaid a sincere Mussulman,
The former calls him a Gueber deserving to be killed.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Zaid, one and the same person, is life to the one,
And to the other an annoyance and a pest.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
If you desire that God may be pleasing to you,
Then look at Him with the eyes of them that love Him.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Look not at that Beauty with your own eyes,
Look at that Object of desire with His votaries' eyes;

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Shut your own eyes from beholding that sweet Object,
And borrow from His admirers their eyes;

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Nay, borrow from Him both eyes and sight,
And with those eyes of His look upon His face,

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
In order that you may not be disappointed with the sight.
God says, "Whoso is God's, God also is his."

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
God says, "I am his eye, his hand, his heart,"
That his good fortune may emerge from adversity.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Whatsoever is hateful to you, if it should lead you
To your beloved, at once becomes agreeable to you.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Why God is named "Hearing," "Seeing" and "Knowing".
God calls himself "Seeing," to the end that

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text: His eye may every moment scare you from sinning.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
God calls himself "Hearing," to the end that
You may close your lips against foul discourse.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
God calls himself "Knowing," to the end that
You may be afraid to plot evil.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
These names are not mere accidental names of God,
As a negro may be called Kafu'r (white);

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
They are names derived from God's essential attributes,
Not mere vain titles of the First Cause.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
For if so, they would be only empty pleasantries,
Like calling the deaf a hearer and the blind a seer,

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Or a name like "impudent" for a modest man,
Or "beautiful" for an ugly negro,

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Or such a title as "Haji" for a new-born boy,
Or that of "Ghazi" applied to a noble idler.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
If such titles as these are used in praising persons
Who do not possess the qualities implied, 'tis wrong;

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
'Twould be jesting or mockery or madness.
"God is exalted above" what is said by evil men.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
I knew you before I met you face to face;
That you had a fair face but an evil heart;

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Yea, I knew you before I saw you,
That you were rooted in iniquity through guile.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
When my eye is red owing to inflammation,
I know 'tis so from the pain, though I see it not.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
You regarded me as a lamb without a shepherd;
You fancied that I had no guardian.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Lovers have suffered chastisement for this cause,
That they have cast ill-timed looks at fair ones.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
They have supposed the fawn to have no shepherd,
They have supposed the captive to be going a begging;

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Till in the twinkling of an eye an arrow pierces them,
Saying, "I am her guardian; look not at her rashly!"

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
What! am I less than a lamb or a fallow deer,
That I should have none to shepherd me?

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Nay, I have a Guardian worthy of dominion,
Who knows every wind that blows upon me.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
He is aware whether that wind is chill or mild,
He is not ignorant nor absent, O mean one.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
The carnal soul is made by God blind and deaf;
I saw with the heart's eye your blindness afar off.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
For this cause I never inquired about you for eight years
Because I saw you filled with ignorance and duplicity.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Why indeed should I inquire about one in the furnace,
Who is bowed down with reproach, like yourself?

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Comparison of the world to a bath stove,
and of piety to the hot bath.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
The lust of the world is like a bath stove,
Whereby the bath of piety is heated;

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
But the lot of the pious is purity from the stove's filth,
Because they dwell in the bath and in cleanliness.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
The rich are as those that carry dung
To heat the furnace of the bath withal.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
God has instilled into them cupidity,
That the bath may be warmed and pleasant.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Quit this stove and push on into the bath;
Know quitting the stove to be the bath itself.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Whoso is in the stove-room is as a servant
To him who is temperate and prudent.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Your lust is as fire in the world,
With a hundred greedy mouths wide open.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
In the judgment of reason this gold is foul dung,
Although, like dung, it serves to kindle the fire.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text:
Whoso was born in the stove-room and never saw purity,
The smell of sweet musk is disagreeable to him.

loc.section: Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story I. The Lover and his Mistress.
text: In illustration of this, a story follows of a tanner who was accustomed to bad smells in the course of his trade, and who was half killed by the smell of musk in the bazaar of the perfumers, but was cured by the accustomed smell of dung.

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text: King David purposed to build a temple at Jerusalem, but was forbidden to do so by a divine voice, because he had been a man of blood. But, it was added, the work should be accomplished by his son Solomon, and Solomon's work would be reckoned the same as David's, in accordance with the texts, "The faithful are brethren," and "Sages are as a single soul," and "We make no distinction between any of the apostles." Accordingly, when Solomon came to the throne, he set about the building, which was attended with many miraculous circumstances, e.g., the stones in the quarry crying out and moving of themselves to the site of the temple. Bilqis, Queen of Saba, sent Solomon a present of forty camels laden with ingots of gold; but Solomon would not receive them, and sent her messengers back with a letter commanding her to abandon the worship of the sun and embrace Islam. At the same time he charged the messengers to report fully to the Queen all they had seen in his kingdom, and to urge her to comply with his commands to renounce her sovereignty and present herself in all humility at his court. As she delayed to come, Solomon again sent to assure her that he had no sinister views regarding her, and desired her attendance at his court solely for her own spiritual benefit. At last Bilqis renounced her royal state and cast away all care for worldly things, and, impelled by earnest desire to learn the true faith, presented herself at the court of King Solomon. Then Solomon commanded that the throne of Bilqis should be brought from Saba, and an 'Afrit offered to fetch it, but Asaf, the vizier anticipated him. Afterwards Solomon proceeded with the building of the temple, wherein he was assisted by devils and fairies. Then God tried Solomon by placing on his throne a false counterpart of him. His miracle working signet was stolen by a devil named Sakhar who thereupon assumed his shape and personated him for forty days, during which Solomon had to wander about and beg his bread. After this he regained his throne, and having completed the temple, began to worship therein. One day he observed that a tuft of coarse grass had sprung up in a corner of the temple, and he was greatly distressed because he thought it portended the ruin of the building, but he took comfort from the thought that while he himself lived the temple would not be allowed to fall into ruin; so long as he lived, at least, he would root up all evil weeds that threatened the safety of the temple, as well the temple built with hands as the spiritual temple in his heart.

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text: In the course of this story, which is told at great length, there occur anecdotes of the beginning of the reign of 'Othman, of the miracles of 'Abdullah Moghrabi, and others, of which abstracts are given below.

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text: Though philosophers call man the microcosm, divines call him the macrocosm.

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
In outward form thou art the microcosm,
But in reality the macrocosm.

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
Seemingly the bough is the cause of the fruit,
But really the bough exists because of the fruit.

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
Were he not impelled by desire of fruit,
The gardener would never have planted the tree.

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
Therefore in reality the tree is born from the fruit,
Though seemingly the fruit is born from the tree.

For this cause Mustafa said, "Adam and all prophets

Though to outward view I am a son of Adam,
In reality I am his first forefather,

Because the angels worshipped him for my sake,

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
Hence in reality our first parent was my offspring,
As in reality the tree is born of its own fruit."

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
What is first in thought is last in act.
Thought is the special attribute of the Eternal.

text:
This product goes forth from heaven very swiftly,
And comes to us like a caravan.

text:
'Tis not a long road that this caravan travels;

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
The heart travels to the Ka'ba every moment,
And by divine grace the body acquires the same power.

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
Distance and nearness affect only the body,
What do they matter in the place where God is?

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
When God changes the body,
It regards not parasangs or miles.

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
Even on earth there is hope of approaching God.
Press on like a lover, and cease vain words, O son!

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text: In the course of his rebuke to the messengers of Bilqis for bringing him mere gold instead of a humble heart, Solomon tells the story of the druggist who used soapstone or Persian earth for a weight. A man came to him to buy sugar-candy, and as he had no weight at hand, he used a lump of soapstone instead; but, while his back was turned, the purchaser stole a bit of the soapstone. The druggist, though he saw what he was doing, would not interrupt him, for he knew that the more soapstone the purchaser stole, the less sugar-candy he would get. In like manner the more men grasp at the transitory wealth of this world, the less they will obtain of the stable wealth of the world to come.

Report to Bilqis what marvels ye have seen,

text:
That she may know Solomon is not covetous of gold;
He has received gold from the Creator of gold.

text:
The moment he wills it, every grain of earth's dust
Is changed into gold and precious pearls.

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
For this cause, O thou that lovest gold,
On the last day God will make earth all silver (white).

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
Quit thy wealth, even if it be the realm of Saba;
Thou wilt find many realms not of this earth.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
What thou callest a throne is only a prison;
Thou thinkest thyself enthroned, but art outside the door.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
Thou hast no sovereignty over thine own passions,
How canst thou sway good and evil?

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
Thy hair turns white without thy concurrence,
Take shame to thyself for thy evil passions.

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
Whoso bows his head to the King of kings
Will receive a hundred kingdoms not of this world;

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
But the delight of bowing down before God
Will seem sweeter to thee than countless glories."

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text: An anecdote follows of a darvesh who saw in a dream some saints, and prayed them to provide him with his daily bread without obliging him to mix in worldly affairs. The saints ordered him to go to the forest, and there he found that all the wild fruits were rendered fit for his food. Having a few grains of gold by him, which he had gained by worldly labour before this miracle had been wrought for him, he was about to give them to a poor woodcutter who was passing that way. But this woodcutter was a saint, and at once read his thoughts, and to show, like Solomon, that he had no need of worldly wealth, he offered up a short prayer to God, and straightway his bundle of firewood was changed into gold, and immediately after, at another prayer, was changed back again into firewood.

text:
Haste to renounce thy kingdom, like Ibrahim bin Adham,
To obtain, like him, the kingdom of eternity.

At night that king would sleep on his throne,

The song of the spheres in their revolutions
Is what men sing with lute and voice.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
The faithful hold that the sweet influences of heaven
Can make even harsh voices melodious.

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.
text:
As we are all members of Adam,

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

But while we are thus shrouded by gross earthly veils,

The fire of love burns hotter under stimulus of music,
Even as occurred in the case of the nut-gatherer.

To the bird with broken wings preach patience,

To the patient well-doer preach comfort and pardon,
To the spiritual 'Anka relate the glories of Mount Qaf,

To the pigeon preach avoidance of the hawk,

display: Masnavi, Book 4, Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

As for the bat, who lingers helpless in the dark,

To the cock the signs of dawning day.

text: Then follows a long account of various miraculous incidents that occurred during the childhood of the Prophet, how he was suckled by Halima, a woman of the Bani Sa'ad, how the idols bowed down before him, how he strayed from home, how his grandfather, Abd ul Muttalib, prayed to God that he might be found, and how he was at last found in the Ka'ba and restored to his grandfather.

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

text: Next a story is told of a cur who attacked a blind man (Kur) in the street, rather than hunt the wild ass (Gor) on the mountains in company with well-bred dogs. This is an illustration of the thesis that mankind is prone to run after mean earthly objects, and to neglect aspiring to the spiritual world.

loc.section: Story II. The Building of the "Most Remote Temple" at Jerusalem.

Arise, Bilqis, now that thou hast the choice,
Before that death lays his heavy hand upon thee.
