display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
You have made these old shoes your object of devotion,
Just as Majnun made an idol of his Laila!

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
You have bound the affection of your soul to them,
And hung them up in your secret chamber.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
How long will you say orisons to this old pair of shoes?
And breathe your oft-told secrets into inanimate ears?

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Like the Arab lover to the house of his dead mistress,
You address to them long invocations of love.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Of what great Asaf were your shoes the house?
Is your old garment, think you, the coat of Yusuf?

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Like a Christian who confesses to a priest
His past year's sins of fornication, fraud, and deceit;

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
In order that the priest may absolve him of those sins;
He thinks the priest's absolution the same as God's!

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
That priest is unable to condemn or to absolve;
But faith and love are a mighty enchantment!

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text: God's dealings visible to the spiritual.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
The wine is from that world, the vessels from this;
The vessels are seen, but the wine is hidden!

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Hidden indeed from the sight of the carnal,
But open and manifest to the spiritual!

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
O God, our eyes are blinded!
O pardon us, our sins are a heavy burden!

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Thou art hidden from us, though the heavens are filled
With Thy light, which is brighter than sun and moon!

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Thou art hidden, yet revealest our hidden secrets!
Thou art the source that causes our rivers to flow.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Thou art hidden in Thy essence, but seen by Thy bounties.
Thou art like the water, and we like the millstone.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Thou art like the wind, and we like the dust;
The wind is unseen, but the dust is seen by all.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Thou art the spring, and we the sweet green garden;
Spring is not seen, though its gifts are seen.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Thou art as the soul, we as hand and foot;
Soul instructs hand and foot to hold and take.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Thou art as reason, we like the tongue;
'Tis reason that teaches the tongue to speak.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Thou art as joy, and we are laughing;
The laughter is the consequence of the joy.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Our every motion every moment testifies,
For it proves the presence of the Everlasting God.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
So the revolution of the millstone, so violent,
Testifies to the existence of a stream of water.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
O Thou who art above our conceptions and descriptions,
Dust be on our heads, and upon our similitudes of Thee!

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Yet Thy slaves never cease devising images of Thee;
They cry to Thee always, "My life is Thy footstool!"

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Like that shepherd who cried," O Lord!
Come nigh to thy faithful shepherd,

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
That he may cleanse thy garment of vermin,
And mend thy shoes, and kiss the hem of thy robe!"

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
No one equaled that shepherd in love and devotion,
Though his manner of expressing it was most faulty.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
His love pitched its tent on the heavens,
He himself was as the dog at the tent-door.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
When the sea of love to God boiled up,
It touched his heart, but it touches your ears only.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text: The thesis that silence may indicate emotions too deep for expression, while eloquent expressions may indicate that the ears only, and not the heart, have been touched, is next illustrated by a ludicrous anecdote of a dwarf who disguised himself as a woman, and presented himself at a sermon addressed to women. This dwarf played a trick on a woman sitting next him, which made her cry out, and the preacher fancied that his sermon had touched her heart; but the dwarf said that if her heart had been touched she would not have betrayed her feelings by publishing them to the whole congregation.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text: The king then again pressed Ayaz to explain the mystery of his regard for the old shoes and rags, in order to admonish the courtiers, for he said that the beauty of true holiness is such that it attracts even infidels. To illustrate this he told an anecdote of a Mosalman who tried to convert a Gueber in the time of Bayazid. The Gueber said that he admired and envied the faith of Bayazid, though he had no power to imitate it; but as for the faith of the missionary who was trying to convert him, it only inspired him with aversion, because it was plainly insincere and hypocritical. And he told an anecdote of a harsh-voiced Mu'azzin who went into a heathen country and there uttered the call to prayer. It happened that there was a girl in that place who had long been inclined to embrace Islam, much to the grief of her parents; but when she heard this harsh call she was at once cured of her wish to forsake her own religion. Her father was so delighted at this that he ran out and loaded the Mu'azzin with gifts. The Gueber said the missionary had cured him of the wish to embrace Islam, just as the girl was cured by the Mu'azzin's harsh voice. But he said he still retained his reverence for the faith of Bayazid, though he failed to understand how so much spirituality as was seen in Bayazid could be contained in an earthly body. He gave a curious illustration of his meaning. A man brought home a piece of meat weighing over half a man, to provide a meal for a guest; but his wife, who was very greedy, ate it all up secretly. When the man missed his meat he asked his wife for it, and she said the cat had eaten it. The man took the cat and weighed her, and found she weighed only half a man. Then he said to his wife, "If this half-man is all cat, where is the meat? and if it is meat, where is the cat?" The Gueber said this was exactly the difficulty he felt about the spirit and the body of Bayazid. He concluded by saying, in the words of the Hadis, "The true believer is attached to others, and others are attached to him, but the hypocrite inspires affection in no one.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text: Mahmud and Ayaz. (continued).

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text: Mahmud again presses Ayaz to reveal his secrets, remarking that even if they suggest sad thoughts, they will benefit the hearers. The wise man is as a guest-house, and he admits all the thoughts that occur to him, whether of joy or of sorrow, with the same welcome, knowing that, like Abraham, he may entertain angels unawares. This is illustrated by the story of a woman who drove away a valued guest by a petulant remark, which he was not intended to hear, and afterwards repented her discourtesy so deeply that she put on mourning and turned her house into an inn. Let grief as well as joy lodge in the heart, for grief is sent for our benefit as well as joy. Endure woe patiently, like Joseph and Job, and regard it as a blessing, saying with Solomon, "Stir me up, O Lord, to be thankful for Thy favor which Thou hast showed upon me!" Mahmud then praises Ayaz for being a true man who can control both lust and anger. Those who are carried away by anger or lust, like the girl of whom an anecdote is told, do not deserve the name of men. When anger or lust takes hold of a man reason departs from him. Then comes an anecdote of a cowardly Sufi who boasted of his bravery, but had not courage enough even to slay a captive infidel. Verily, the "greater warfare," viz., that against one's own lusts and passions, demands as much courage as the "lesser warfare" against the infidels. This is illustrated by a story of a saint named Iyazi, who, after having been a great warrior against the infidels, renounced the world and applied himself to wage the "greater warfare" against his own lusts. One day, while sitting in his cell, he heard the noise of the army going out to fight, and his carnal passion urged him to go and join in the fight, but he thus rebuked it:

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text: Iyazi's rebuke to his passion, whish lusted to join in the "lesser warfare".

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
I said, "O foul and faithless passion,
Whence have you derived this inclination to war?

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Tell me truly, O passion, is this your trickery?
Or else is it stubbornness shunning obedience to God?

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
If you say not truly I will attack you,
And will afflict you more severely with discipline."

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Passion then heaved a cry from its breast,
And without mouth vented the following complaints:

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
"In this cell you slay me every day;
You slay my life like the life of a Gueber.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Not a soul is aware of my condition;
You drag me along without food or sleep.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
In the fight with one wound I shall quit the body,
And the people will admire my valor and self-devotion."

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
I said, "O bad passion, you live as an infidel,
And as an infidel you will die; shame be upon you!

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
In both worlds you are naught but a hypocrite;
In the two worlds only an unprofitable servant.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
I have vowed to God never to quit this cell
While life remains in this body;

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Because whatever the body does in this privacy
Is not done to make a fair show before men.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Its movements and its rest in the privacy of this cell
Are not intended for the sight of any besides God.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
This is the 'greater warfare,' that the 'lesser;'
Both these warfares have their Rustams and Haidars.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
They are not to be fought by one whose reason and sense
Flee away as soon as a mouse wags its tail.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Such persons must shun the array of battle,
And keep aloof from it even as women do."

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text: This is followed by an anecdote of another brave warrior who "was among the faithful, and made good what he had promised to God." Then comes a long story of a prince of Egypt who saw the portrait of a damsel belonging to the Chief of Mausil, and conceived an ardent passion for her, and sent an army to take her by force. The army succeeded in capturing her, and set out on the return march; but on the way the captain of the army fell in love with the damsel, and she returned his affection. When they reached Egypt she was made over to the prince, but at once took a dislike to him, as he was not nearly so manly as her beloved captain. The prince discovered her secret, and though he might justly have resented the treachery of the captain, he refrained, and showed true manliness in the "greater warfare" by pardoning his fault and uniting him with the damsel to whom he was so much attached.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text: Ideas gained from hearing a thing lead to seeing it.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
A person put this question to a philosopher,
"O sage, what is true and what is false?"

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
The sage touched his ear and said, "This is false,
But the eye is true and its report is certain."

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
The ear is false in relation to the eye,
And most assertions are related to the ear.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
If a bat turn away its eyes from the sun,
Still it is not veiled from some idea of the sun;

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Its very dread of the sun frames an idea of the sun,
And that idea scares it away to the darkness.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
That idea of light terrifies it,
And makes it cling to the murky night.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Just so 'tis your idea of your terrible foe
Which makes you cling to your friends and allies.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
O Moses, thy revelations shed glory on the mount,
But that frightened one endured not thy realities.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Be not too proud, but know that you must first endure
The idea of the Truth, and thence come to the reality.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
No one is frightened by the mere idea of fighting,
For "no courage is needed before fighting begins."

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
In the mere idea of fighting a coward can imagine
Himself as attacking and retreating like Rustam.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
The pictures of Rustam on the wall of a bath
Are similar to a coward's ideas of fighting.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
But when these ideas are tested by actual sight,
What of the coward then? His bravery is gone!

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Strive, then, from mere hearing to press on to seeing;
What ear has told you falsely eye will tell truly.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Then ear too will acquire the properties of an eye;
Your ears, now worthless as wool, will become gems;

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Yea, your whole body will become a mirror,
It will be as an eye or a bright gem in your bosom.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
First the hearing of the ear enables you to form ideas,
Then these ideas guide you to the Beloved.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Strive, then, to increase the number of these ideas,
That they may guide you, like Majnun, to the Beloved.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text: Concerning the unbelievers who say, "There is only this our present life; we live and we die, and naught but time destroyeth us."

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
To return; that prince played the fool,
And took delight in the society of the damsel.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
O prince, suppose your dominion extend from east to west,
Yet, as it endures not, esteem it transitory as lightning

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Yea, O sleeping heart, know the kingdom that endures not
Forever and ever is only a mere dream.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
I marvel how long you will indulge in vain illusion,
Which has seized you by the throat like a headsman.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Know that even in this world there is a place of refuge;
Hearken not to the unbeliever who denies it.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
His argument is this: he says again and again,
"If there were aught beyond this life we should see it."

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
But if the child sees not the state of reason,
Does the man of reason therefore forsake reason?

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
And if the man of reason sees not the state of love,
Is the blessed moon of love thereby eclipsed?

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
The beauty of Joseph was not visible to his brethren;
Was it therefore hidden from the eyes of Jacob?

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
The eyes of Moses regarded his staff as a stick,
But the divine eye saw it to be a deadly serpent.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
The eye of the head was at issue with the divine eye,
But the latter prevailed and gave convincing proof.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
To the eyes of Moses his hand looked a mere hand,
But to the divine eye it appeared a flashing light.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
This subject in its entirety is endless,
But to the unbeliever it is a mere fanciful idea.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
The only realities to him are lust and gluttony;
Speak not then to him of the mysteries of the Beloved.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
To us believers lust and gluttony are only ideas,
Therefore we behold always the beauty of the Beloved.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
To all men whose creed is lust and gluttony,
Applies the text, "To you be your creed, to me mine."

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
In the face of negations like these cut short speech,
"O Ahmad, say little to an old Fire-worshipper!"

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text: "We distribute among them," to some carnal lusts, and to others angelic qualities.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
If the prince lacked the animal manliness of asses,
Yet he possessed the true manliness of the prophets.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
He renounced lust and anger and concupiscence,
And showed himself a man of the lineage of the prophets.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Grant that he lacked the virility of asses,
Yet God esteemed him a lord of lords.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Let me be dead, so long as God regards me with favor!
I am better off than the living who are rejected of God;

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
The former is the kernel of manliness, the latter only the rind;
The former is borne to Paradise, the latter to hell.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
The Prophet says, "Paradise is annexed to tribulation,
But hell-fire follows indulgence in lust."

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
O Ayaz, who slayest demons like a male lion,
Manliness of asses is naught, manliness of mind much.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
What sort of man dost thou think him who sports as a boy,
But who has no comprehension of these chief matters?

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
o thou who hast seen the delight of my connnandments,
And risked thy life to perform them faithfully,

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text:
Hear a tale of the sweetness of my commandments,
That the meaning of this sweetness may be made plain.

loc.section: Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.

display: Masnavi, Book 5, Story VIII. (continued). Mahmud and Ayaz.
text: The story which follows is one in which Ayaz is himself the chief actor, and hence it may perhaps be inferred that this part of the poem had not received its final revision when the poet died. The king showed to all his courtiers in turn a valuable jewel, and asked them its value. Each declared it to be priceless. He thereupon ordered each of them to break it to pieces, but they refused, one after the other; on which he praised them highly and gave them presents. Finally the jewel came into the hands of Ayaz, and he, not being a mere imitator like the rest, nor being tempted by the rewards given to the rest, decided that the king's command ought to be obeyed at all costs, and therefore broke the jewel to pieces. Blind imitation of current fashions and ruling "public opinion" is the way of the world, but its worthlessness is at once manifested when it is put to the test. True faith is a reasonable faith, not one adopted and held in mechanical and parrot-like fashion. The king then commanded that those courtiers whose faith had been shown to be mere "taqlid" or imitation, and not vital and intelligent, should be put to death; but Ayaz interceded for them, saying, "O Lord, punish them not if they forget or fall into sin;" although their plea that they sinned through forgetfulness is of no more weight than the plea of having sinned through drunkenness, seeing that both forgetfulness and drunkenness are willfully incurred. Those who die in amity with God have no cause to fear death, "It cannot harm them, for to their Lord will they return;" but those who die at enmity with God are in a very different position, and have therefore a very strong claim for mercy. The Egyptian magicians, when threatened by Pharaoh with death for believing in Moses, recognized the truth that death in such a cause would unite them with God, and that extinction of the phenomenal self, on which Pharaoh prided himself, would bring them to the real Self from whom they had been estranged by life on earth. Like Habib, the carpenter of Antioch, who was martyred for taking the part of 'Isa's two apostles in that city, they said, "O that my people knew how gracious God hath been to me, and that He hath made me one of His honored ones!" A man can only say "I" with truth when he has mortified self and unlearnt to say "I" in the sense in which Pharaoh said it. Fakhru-'d-Din Razi discoursed learnedly on this point, saying much of "incarnation" and "union" as the modes in which the real "I" of the Deity indwells in the human soul; but as he lacked the true mystic unction, his words only serve to darken counsel. But here Ayaz breaks off; saying, "Who am I that I should say to the Almighty, 'Grant pardon to these offenders'?" The Omniscient God needs not to be informed of their case, for He knows all; nor to be reminded of it, for He forgets nothing; nor to be urged to act mercifully, for He created men "for their own benefit, and not to derive benefit from them." Such intercession, therefore, implies ignorance of God, and "such only of His servants as are possessed of knowledge of God truly fear God." God is at once center and circumference of the universe, and the only true wisdom consists in absolute self-surrender to His will, and this surrender of self will bring with it its own exceeding great reward.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text: Prologue

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
O LIFE of the heart, Husamu-'d-Din,:
My zeal burnt within me to write this sixth part!

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
The Masnavi became a standard through thy influence,
Thy sword (Husam) has made it an exemplar to the world

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
O spiritual one, I now offer it to thee,
This sixth part of the entire Masnavi.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Enlighten the world's six sides with its six parts,
That it may illuminate him who is not illuminated!

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Love has naught to do with five senses or six sides,
Its only aim is to be attracted to the Beloved!

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
But haply leave may be given me hereafter
To tell those mysteries so far as they can be told,

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
In a discourse more closely approximating to the facts
Than these faint indications of those abstruse matters.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Mysteries are not communicable, save to those who know;
Mystery in the ear of infidels is no mystery.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Nevertheless, this is a call to you from God;
It matters not to Him whether ye accept or reject it.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Noah repeated His call for nine hundred years,
But his people only increased in rebellion.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Never did he draw back from admonishing them,
Never did he retire into the cave of silence.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
He said, "At the barking and howling of the dogs
No caravan ever turned back in its road.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Nor does the full moon on a bright night cease shining
Because of the howling of dogs on earth.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
The moon sheds her light, and the dogs howl;
Every one acts according to his nature.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
To each one his office is allotted by the divine decree,
And he acts agreeably to his nature."

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Art thou thirsting for the Ocean of spirituality?
Disport thyself on this island of the Masnavi!

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Disport thyself so long as thou seest every moment
Spiritual verities revealed in this Masnavi.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
When the wind blows the grass off the water,
The water then shows forth its own purity.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Behold the bright and fresh sprays of coral,
And the princely fruits growing in the water of life!

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
So, when the Masnavi is purged of letters and words,
It drops all these, and appears as the sea of Unity.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Then speaker and hearer and spoken words
All three give up the ghost in that consummation.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Bread-giver and bread-eater and bread itself
Are purified of their forms and turn to dust.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
But their essences in each of these three grades
Are distinguished, as in those states, so eternally.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Their form turns to dust, but their essence not;
If one says it does, tell him it does not.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
In the world of spirits all three await judgment,
Sometimes wearing their earthly forms, sometimes not.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text: The worth of a man depends on the objects of his aspiration.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
One day a student asked a preacher,
Saying, "O most orthodox ornament of the pulpit,

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
I have a question to ask, O lord of learning;
Tell me the answer to it in this congregation.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
A bird sat on the top of a wall;
Which was best, its head or its tail?"

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
He replied, "If its face was towards the town,
And its tail to the villages, then its face was best.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
But if its tail was towards the town, and its face
Towards the villages, then prefer its tail to its face."

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
A bird flies with its wings towards its nest,
The wings of a man are his aspiration and aim.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
If a lover be befouled with good and evil,
Yet regard not these; regard rather his aspiration.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Though a falcon be all white and unmatched in form,
If he hunts mice he is contemptible and worthless.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
And if an owl fixes his affection on the king,
He is a falcon in reality; regard not his outward form.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Adam's clay was kneaded in the limits of a trough,
Yet was he exalted above heaven and stars.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
"We have honored Adam" was not addressed to the sky,
But to Adam himself full of defects as he was.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Did one ever propose to earth or heaven to receive
Beauty, reason, speech and aspiration?

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Would you ever offer to the heavens
Beauty of face and acuteness of thought?

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
O son, did you ever present your silver body
As an offering to the damsels pictured on bath walls?

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Nay, you pass by those pictures though fair as Huris,
And offer yourself sooner to half-blind old women.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
What is there in the old women which the pictures lack,
Which draws you from the pictures to the old women?

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Say not, for I will say it in plain words,
'Tis reason, sense, perception, thought, and life.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
In the old woman life is infused,
While the pictures of the bath have no life.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
If the pictures of the bath should stir with life (soul),
They would uproot your love to all the old women.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
What is soul? 'Tis acquainted with good and evil,
Rejoicing at pleasant things, grieving at His.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Since, then, the principle of soul is knowledge,
He who knows most is most full of soul.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Knowledge is the effect flowing from soul;
He who has most of it is most godlike.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Seeing then, beloved, that knowledge is the mark of soul,
He who knows most has the strongest soul.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
The world of souls is itself entirely knowledge,
And he who is void of knowledge is void of soul.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
When knowledge is lacking in a man s nature,
His soul is like a stone on the plain.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Primal Soul is the theatre of God's court,
Soul of souls the exhibition of God Himself.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
All the angels were pure reason and soul,
Yet when the new soul of Adam came, they were as its body.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
When in joy they crowded round that new soul,
They bowed before it as body does before soul.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text: Fear of men's censure the greatest obstacle to acceptance of the true faith.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
O Husamu-'d-Din, I might tell some of thy many virtues,
Were it not for the fear of the evil eyes.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
From evil eyes and malice-empoisoned breaths
Already have I suffered fatal wounds.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Therefore I cannot relate thy ecstatic states,
Save by hints of the ecstatic states of others.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
This manoeuvre is one of the devices of the heart,
Whereby the heart's feet wend their way to the truth.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Many hearts and souls would become lovers of God
Did not evil eyes or evil ears hold them back.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Of these Abu Talib, the Prophet's uncle, was one;
The malice of the Arabs scared him from the faith.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
He said, "What will the Arabs say of me?
That my own nephew has perverted me from my religion!"

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Muhammad said, "O uncle, confess the faith to me,
That I may strive with God for thee!"

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
He said, "Nay; it will be published by them that hear;
'A secret known to more than two is known to every one.'

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
As I live in the midst of these Arabs,
It will cause me to lose caste with them.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Yet, had the mighty grace of God led the way,
How could this fear have vied with God's attraction?

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
O Granter of aid, lend us aid
In this dilemma of the feeble will.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text: Prayers for right guidance in the use of free will, which gift was refused by heavens and earth, but accepted by man to his own.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
This flux and reflux of resolves came to me from Thee,
Else these tides of will had rested still, O God!

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
By the same fiat whereby Thou madest me thus irresolute,
Of Thy mercy deliver me from this irresolution!

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Thou triest me; O give me aid!
For men are as women through this trial.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
How long, O Lord, is this trial to last?
Give me one ruling principle, not ten principles!

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
The whole world flees away from its own will and being
Towards self-abandonment and intoxication.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
In order to escape a while from self-consciousness,
Men incur the reproach of wine and strong drink;

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
For all know well this existence is a snare,
This thought and memory and will only a hell.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Therefore they flee from self to being beside themselves,
Call it intoxication or call it preoccupation, O guided one.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
Ere it is annihilated, no single soul
Finds admittance to the divine hall of audience.

loc.section: Prologue

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Prologue
text:
What is "ascension" to heaven? Annihilation of self;
Self-abandonment is the creed and religion of lovers.

loc.section: Story I. The Hindu Slave who loved his Master's Daughter.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story I. The Hindu Slave who loved his Master's Daughter.
text: Story I. The Hindu Slave who loved his Master's Daughter.

loc.section: Story I. The Hindu Slave who loved his Master's Daughter.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story I. The Hindu Slave who loved his Master's Daughter.
text: A certain man had a Hindu slave, whom he had brought up along with his children, one of whom was a daughter. When the time came for giving the girl in marriage many suitors presented themselves, and offered large marriage portions to gain her alliance. At last her father selected one who was by no means the richest or noblest of the number, but pious and well-mannered. The women of the family would have preferred one of the richer youths, but the father insisted on having his own way, and the marriage was settled according to his wishes. As soon as the Hindu slave heard of this he fell sick, and the mistress of the family discovered that he was in love with her daughter, and aspired to the honor of marrying her. She was much discomposed at this unfortunate accident, and consulted her husband as to what was best to be done. He said, "Keep the affair quiet, and I will cure the slave of his presumption, in such a way that, according to the proverb, 'The Shaikh shall not be burnt, yet the meat shall be well roasted.'" He directed his wife to flatter the slave with the hope that his wish would be granted, and the girl given to him in marriage. He then celebrated a mock marriage between the slave and the girl, but at night substituted for the girl a boy dressed in female attire, with the result that the bridegroom passed the night in quarrelling with his supposed bride. Next morning he had an interview with the girl and her mother, and said he would have no more to do with her, as, though her appearance was very seductive at a distance, closer acquaintance with her had altogether destroyed the charm. Just so the pleasures of the world seem sweet till they are tried, and then they are found to be very bitter and repulsive. The Prophet has declared that "Patience is the key of joy;" in other words, that he who controls and restrains himself from grasping at worldly pleasures will find true happiness; but this precept makes no lasting impression on the bulk of mankind. When bitter experience overtakes them, as the pain of burning afflicts children, or moths sporting with fire, or the pain of amputation a thief, they curse the delusive temptations which brought this pain upon them; but no sooner is the pain abated than they run after the same pleasures as eagerly as ever. This is divinely ordained, that "God may bring to naught the craft of the infidels." Their hearts have, as it were, been kindled on the tinder-box of bitter experience, but God has put out the sparks of good resolution, and caused them to forget their experience and vows of abstinence according to the text, "Often as they kindle a beacon-fire for war doth God quench it." This is illustrated by an anecdote of a man who heard a footstep in his house at night, and at once struck a light; but the thief put it out without being observed, and the man remained under the impression that it had gone out of itself. This leads the poet again to dwell on his favorite theme of the sole agency of Allah.

loc.section: Story I. The Hindu Slave who loved his Master's Daughter.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story I. The Hindu Slave who loved his Master's Daughter.
text: Then, to supply the necessary corrective of this doctrine, another anecdote is told concerning Mahmud and Ayaz. The courtiers grumbled because Ayaz received the stipend of thirty courtiers, and Mahmud by a practical test convinced them that the talents of Ayaz equalled those of thirty men. The courtiers replied that this was due to God's grace, not to any merit on the part of Ayaz; and the king confuted them by pointing out that man's responsibility and merit, or demerit, for his actions are recognized in the Koran. Iblis was condemned for saying to God, "Thou hast caused me to err," and Adam was commended or saying, "We have blackened ourselves." And elsewhere it is said, "Whosoever shall have wrought an atom's weight of good shall behold it; and whoso shall have wrought an atom's weight of evil shall behold it."

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text: A fowler went out to catch birds, and disguised himself by wrapping his head up in leaves and grass, so as to avoid frightening the birds away from his snare. A bird of some sagacity came near him, and suspected something wrong, but foolishly lingered near, and began to question him as to his business. The fowler said he was a hermit who had retired from the world and dressed himself in weeds for the health of his soul. The bird said he was surprised to see a Mosalman doing this in contravention of the Prophet's precept, "There is no monkery in Islam," and his repeated declarations that Islam involves association with the faithful and avoidance of a solitary life. The fowler replied that a solitary life was allowed in heathen countries for the soul's health. The bird then asked what the grains of wheat were that were strewed on the trap. The fowler replied that they were the property of an orphan, which had been deposited with him in consequence of his known probity. The bird then asked permission to eat some, as he was very hungry, and the fowler, with much pretended reluctance, allowed him to do so. The moment he touched the grain the trap closed upon him, and he found himself a prisoner. He then abused the fowler for his trickery, but the fowler said he had only himself to blame for his greediness in eating the food which belonged to an orphan. The moral is, that it is not destiny which leads people into afflictions, but their own errors and vices.

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text: The bird's cries to God for aid.

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
When he had eaten the grain he was caught in the trap,
And began to recite the chapters "Yasin" and "An'am."

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
Then he began to wail and cry loudly,
So that the very fowler and his trap shook with grief.

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
He said, "My back is broken by the conflict of my thoughts;
O Beloved One, come and stroke my head in mercy!

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
The palm of Thy hand on my head gives me rest,
Thy hand is a sign of Thy bounteous providence.

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
Remove not Thy shadow from my head,
I am afflicted, afflicted, afflicted!

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
Sleep has deserted my eyes
Through my longing for Thee, O Envy of cypresses!

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
Though I be unworthy of Thy favor, how were it
If thou shouldst regard the grieves of unworthy me?

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
What claim of right can a non-existent thing make
To have the doors of Thy bounty opened to it?

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
Yet Thy bounty had regard to my senseless dust
And endued it with the ten jewels of the senses

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
Five external senses and five internal senses,
Whereby inanimate seed became a living man.

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
O Light on high! what is repentance without Thy grace
But a mere mockery of the beard of repentance;

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
Thou rootest up the hairs of such repentance,
Repentance is the shadow, Thou the shining Moon.

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
Alas! Thou hast ruined my house and home;
How can I cease wailing while Thou oppressest me?

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
How can I flee away when there is no living away?
Without Thy sustaining lordship there is no slave.

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
O take my life, Thou that art the source of life!
For apart from Thee I am wearied of my life.

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
I am a lover well versed in lovers' madness,
I am weary of learning and sense.

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
Since my bashfulness is destroyed, I will publish secrets;
How long must I bear this trepidation and anxiety?

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
Formerly I was covered by modesty as by a veil,
Now I will leap from it under Thy coverlet!

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
O comrades, our Beloved has closed up all paths;
We are as lame deer, and He as a raging lion.

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text:
Say what remedy is there but resignation
When one is fallen into the hands of the raging lion?"

loc.section: Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story II. The Fowler and the Bird.
text: The poet then passes on to the subject of the need for constant watchfulness, in order to avoid the snares of the world, and not to miss the divine blessing whenever it may appear. There is a tradition, "When half the night has passed Allah will descend to earth, and cry, 'Ho, ye that ask, it shall be answered to you; and ye that crave pardon, it shall be pardoned to you; and ye that petition, your petitions shall be granted.'" But all who sleep the sleep of negligence will miss the promised blessing. This is illustrated by the story of a lover who obtained an assignation with his mistress, but when she came, was found asleep, and was accordingly rejected.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text: Then follow exhortations to undergo "the pains of negation," as they are called in the Gulshan i Raz, i.e., even as the great saint and poet Faridu-'d-Din 'Attar cast away his drugs, to cast one's own will, knowledge, power, and "self" into the unique river of "annihilation," and from that state to rise to the higher state of eternal existence in God. The end and object of all negation is to attain to subsequent affirmation, as the negation in the creed, "There is no God," finds its complement and purpose in the affirmation "but God." Just so the purpose of negation of self is to clear the way for the apprehension of the fact that there is no existence but The One. The intoxication of life and its pleasures and occupations veils the Truth from men's eyes, and they ought to pass on to the spiritual intoxication which makes men beside themselves and lifts them to the beatific vision of eternal Truth. This is the same thing as saying they must pass on from negation to affirmation, from ignorance to the highest knowledge. This is illustrated by the story of the Turkish noble and the minstrel, which is given with an apology for using illustrations derived from drunkenness. A Turkish noble awoke from his drunken sleep, and called his minstrel to enliven him. The minstrel was a spiritual man, and proceeded to improve the occasion by singing a song with a deep spiritual meaning:

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
"I know not if thou art a moon or an idol,
I know not what thou requirest of me.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
I know not what service to pay thee,
Whether to keep silence or to speak.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
Thou art not apart from me, yet, strange to say,
I know not where I am, or where thou art.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
I know not wherefore thou art dragging me,
Now embracing me, and now wounding me!"

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text: Thus the whole of his song consisted of repetitions of the words, "I know not." At last the noble could endure it no longer, and he took a stick and threatened to beat the minstrel, saying, "O wretch, tell us something you do know, and do not repeat what you do not know. if I ask you whence you come or what you have eaten, and you answer only by negations, your answer is a waste of time. Say what you mean by all these negations." The minstrel replied, "My meaning is a concealed one. I fear to make affirmations in opposition to your negations, so I state negations that you may get a hint of the corresponding affirmations from them. I now hint the truth to you in my song; and when death comes to you, you will learn the mysteries which at present I can only hint."

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text: Spiritual mysteries set forth in the Masnavi under similes of intoxication.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
That wine of God is gained from that minstrel,
This bodily wine from this minstrel.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
Both of these have one and the same name in speech,
But the difference between their worth is great.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
Men's bodies are like pitchers with closed mouths;
Beware, till you see what is inside them.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
The pitcher of this body holds the water of life,
Whilst that one holds deadly poison.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
If you look at the contents you are wise;
If you look only at the vessel you are misguided.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
Know words resemble these bodies,
And the meaning resembles the soul.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
The body's eyes are ever intent on bodies,
The soul's eyes on the reasonable soul;

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
Wherefore, in the figures of the words of the Masnavi,
The form misleads, but the inner meaning guides.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
In the Koran it is declared that its parables
"Mislead some and guide some."

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
O God! when a spiritual man talks of wine,
How can a fellow spiritual man mistake his meaning?

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
Thus that minstrel began his intoxicating song,
"O give me Thy cup, Thou whom I see not!

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
Thou art my face; what wonder if I see it not?
Extreme nearness acts as an obscuring veil.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
Thou art my reason; what wonder if I see Thee not
Through the multitude of intervening obstacles?

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
Thou art 'nearer to me than my neck vein,'
How can I call to Thee, 'Ho,' as if thou wert far off?

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
Nay, but I will mislead some by calling in the desert,
To hide my Beloved from those of whom I am jealous!"

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text: This is illustrated by an anecdote of the Prophet and Ayisha. Ayisha was once sitting with the Prophet without her veil, when a blind man came in. Ayisha, knowing well the jealous disposition of her husband, at once prepared to retire on which the Prophet said, "The man is blind and cannot see you." Ayisha replied by signs that though the man could not see her she could see him. Just so the spiritual man is jealous of exposing his mysteries to the gaze of the profane, and from excess of caution veils them in signs and hints.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text: Then comes a commentary on the tradition, "Die before you die," i.e., mortify your carnal passions and lusts, and deny and annihilate your carnal " self" before the death of the body overtakes you. Men who put off repentance till they are at the point of death are likened to the Shi'as of Aleppo, who every year on the Ashura, or tenth day of Muharram, meet at the Antioch gate to bewail the martyrdom of Hasan and Husain. Once, while they were thus engaged, a Sunni poet arrived at the city, and inquired the reason of this excessive grief and mourning. The Shi'as rebuked him for his ignorance of sacred history, and he said, "This martyrdom happened a long time ago; but it would seem, from your excessive grief, that the news of it has only just reached you. You must have been sleeping all this time not to have heard it before, and now you are mourning for your own sleepiness!" To the truly spiritual, who have drunk of God's wine and bear the "tokens of it on their foreheads," death is an occasion for rejoicing, not for wailing. The man who is engrossed with the trifling pleasures of the world and blind to the ample provision made for the soul is like an ant in a barn of wheat, toiling to carry off a single grain, when ample stores of wheat are already at its disposal. Spiritual men must continue urging the worldly to repent and avail themselves of this heavenly provision for their souls, careless, like Noah, whether their preaching is listened to or not. This is illustrated by an anecdote of a man who knocked at the door of an empty house at midnight, in order to give notice that it was time to prepare the meal taken at dawn in Ramazan.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text: Reason for knocking at the empty house.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
You have said your say; now hear my answer,
So as not to remain in astonishment and bewilderment.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
Though to you this time seems midnight,
To me the dawn of joyful morn seems nigh.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
To the vulgar all parts of the world seem dead,
But to God they are instinct with sense and love.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
And as to your saying that "this house is empty,
Why then should I beat a drum before it?"

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
Know that the people of God expend money,
And build many mosques and holy places,

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
And spend health and wealth in distant pilgrimages,
In ecstatic delight, like intoxicated lovers;

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
And none of them ever say, "The Ka'ba is empty;"
How can one who knows the truth say that?

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
These people are ranged in battle array,
And risk their lives to gain God's favor;

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
One plunged in calamities like Job himself,
Another exhibiting patience like Jacob.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
Thousands of them are thirsty and afflicted,
Striving in earnest desire to do God's will.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
I likewise, in order to please the merciful God,
Beat my drum at every door in hope of dawn.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
Seek ye a purchaser who will pay you gold;
Where will you find one more liberal than God?

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
He buys the worthless rubbish which is your wealth,
He pays you the light that illumines your heart.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
He accepts these frozen and lifeless bodies of yours,
And gives you a kingdom beyond what you dream of.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
He takes a few drops of your tears,
And gives you the divine fount sweeter than sugar.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
He takes your sighs fraught with grief and sadness,
And for each sigh gives rank in heaven as interest.

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
In return for the sigh-wind that raised tear-clouds,
God gave Abraham the title of "Father of the faithful."

loc.section: Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story III. The Drunken Turkish Amir and the Minstrel.
text:
Come! in this incomparable and crowded mart
Sell your old goods and take a kingdom in payment!

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text: To illustrate the rich recompense that is awarded to those who are faithful in tribulation, the story of Bilal is next recounted at length. Bilal was an Abyssinian slave belonging to a Jew of Mecca, and had incurred his master's displeasure in consequence of having embraced Islam. For this offence his master tortured him by exposing him to the heat of the midday sun, and beating him with thorns. But notwithstanding his anguish, Bilal would not recant his faith, and uttered only the cry, "Ahad, Ahad!" "The One, the One God!" At this moment Abu Bakr, the "Faithful witness," happened to pass by, and was so struck by his constancy that he resolved to buy him of the Jew. After much higgling and attempts at cheating on the Jew's part he succeeded in doing so, and at once set him free. When the Prophet heard of this purchase he said to Abu Bakr, "Give me a share in him;" but Abu Bakr told him, somewhat to his annoyance, that he had already set him free. Notwithstanding this Bilal attached himself to the Prophet, and was afterwards promoted to the honourable post of the Prophet's Mu'azzin.

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text: This is followed by the story of Hilal, another holy man who, like Bilal and Luqman and Joseph, served a noble in the capacity of groom. His affections were set on things above, and he was ever pressing upwards towards the high mark of spiritual exaltation, and saying, like Moses, "I will not stop till I reach the confluence of the two seas, and for years will I journey on." Herein he presented a great contrast to ordinary men, who are ever giving way to their lusts, and so being dragged down into the state of mere animals, or even lower. Hilal's master was a Mosalman, yet one whose eyes were only partially open to the truth. He was in the habit of asking his guests their age; and if they answered doubtfully, saying, "Perhaps eighteen, or seventeen, or sixteen, or even fifteen," he would rebuke them, saying, "As you seem to be putting yourself lower and lower, you had better go back at once to your mother's womb." These guests are a type of men who lower themselves from the rank of humanity to that of animals. This master, however, was blind to Hilal's spiritual excellence, and allowed him to drag on a miserable existence in his stables. At last Hilal fell sick; but no one cared for him, till the Prophet himself, warned by a divine intimation, came to visit him, and commiserated his wretched condition. Hilal proved himself to be faithful through tribulation; for, instead of grumbling at his lot, he replied, "How is that sleep wretched which is broken by the advent of the Sun of prophecy? or how can he be called athirst on whose head is poured the water of life?" In truth, Hilal had by degrees become purified from the stain of earthly existence and earthly qualities, and washed in the fountain of the water of life, i.e., the holy revelations of the Prophet, till he had attained the exalted grade of purity enjoined on those who would study God's Word aright.

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text:
Growth in grace is accomplished by slow degrees, and not per saltum.
Since you have told the story of Hilal (the new moon)

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text: Now set forth the story of Badr (the full moon).

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text:
That new moon and that full moon are now united,
Removed from duality and defect and shortcomings.

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text:
That Hilal is now exalted above inward defect;
His outward defects served as degrees of ascension.

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text:
Night after night that mentor taught him grades of ascent
And through his patient waiting gave him happiness.

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text:
The mentor says, "O raw hastener, through patient waiting,
You must climb to the summit step by step.

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text:
Boil your pot by degrees and in a masterly way;
Food boiled in mad haste is spoiled.

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text:
Doubtless God could have created the universe
By the fiat 'Be!' in one moment of time;

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text:
Why, then, did He protract His work over six days,
Each of which equaled a thousand years, O disciple?

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text:
Why does the formation of an infant take nine months?
Because God's method is to work by slow degrees,

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text:
Why did the formation of Adam take forty days?
Because his clay was kneaded by slow degrees.

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text:
Not hurrying on like you, O raw one,
Who claim to be a Shaikh whilst yet only a child!

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text:
You run up like a gourd higher than all plants,
But where is your power of resistance or combat?

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text:
You have leant on trees or on walls,
And so mounted up like a gourd, O little dog rose;

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text:
Even though your prop may be a lofty cypress,
At last you are seen to be dry and hollow.

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text:
O gourd, your bright green hue soon turns yellow.
For it is not a natural but an artificial color."

loc.section: Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story IV. The Purchase of Bilal.
text: This is illustrated by an anecdote of an ugly old hag who painted her face to make it look pretty, but was detected and exposed to scorn.

loc.section: Story V. The Sufi and the Qazi.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story V. The Sufi and the Qazi.
text: Story V. The Sufi and the Qazi.

loc.section: Story V. The Sufi and the Qazi.

display: Masnavi, Book 6, Story V. The Sufi and the Qazi.
text: A sick man laboring under an incurable disease went to a physician for advice. The physician felt his pulse, and perceived that no treatment would cure him, and therefore told him to go away and do whatever he had a fancy for. This was the advice given by God to the Israelites when they were seen to be incurable by the admonitions of the prophets. "Do what you will, but God's eye is on all your doings." The sick man blessed the physician for his agreeable prescription, and at once went to a stream, where he saw a Sufi bathing his feet. He was seized with a desire to hit the Sufi on the back, and, calling to mind the physician's advice, at once carried his wish into effect. The Sufi jumped up, and was about to return the blow, but when he saw the weakly and infirm condition of his assailant he restrained himself. He disregarded his present angry impulse, and had regard to the future, so that the non-existent future became to him more really existent than the existing present. Here the poet digresses to point out that when wise men recognize the true relative importance of the present and the future they cease to shrink from death and annihilation, which lifts them to a higher and nobler life. This is illustrated by an anecdote of Mahmud of Ghazni, quoted from Faridu- 'd-Din 'Attar. Mahmud, in one of his campaigns, took prisoner a Hindu boy, who at first regarded him with the greatest dread, in consequence of the stories he had heard of him from his mother, but afterwards experienced Mahmud's kindness and tenderness, and came to know him and love him. So it is with death. According to the Hadis "Those who have passed away do not grieve because of death, but because of wasted opportunities in life." The Masnavi is "a shop of poverty and self-abnegation," and a treasury containing only the doctrines of "Unity;" and if its stories suggest aught else, that is due to the evil promptings of Iblis, who also misled the Prophet himself to attribute undue power to the idols Lat and 'Uzza and Manat, in a verse which was afterwards cancelled. The Sufi, being full of the spirit of self-abnegation, did not retaliate on his weak, assailant but led him before the Qazi. On learning the facts of the case the Qazi said, "This Faqir is sick to death, and you, being a Sufi, are, according to your profession, dead to the world. How, then, can I award a penalty against him in your favor? I am a judge, not of the dead, but of the living." The Sufi was dissatisfied with this view of the case, and again pressed the Qazi to do him justice. On this the Qazi asked the sick Faqir how much money he had, and on his replying, "Six dirhams," took pity on him, and let him off with a fine of three dirhams only. The moment the sentence was pronounced the sick Faqir went up to the Qazi and struck him a blow on the back, and cried out, "Now take the other three dirhams and let me go!" The Sufi then pointed out to the Qazi that by his ill-timed leniency to the Faqir he had brought this blow upon himself, and urged him to apply in his own case those principles of mercy and forgiveness which he had proposed in the case of another. The Qazi said that, for his part, he recognized every blow and misfortune that might befall him as divinely ordained, and sent for his good, according to the text, "Laugh little and weep much," and that his judgment in the matter of the Faqir had not been dictated by impulse, but by inspiration. The Sufi again asked him how evils and misfortunes could proceed from the divine fount of good, and the Qazi replied that what seems good and evil to us has no absolute existence, but is merely as the foam on the surface of the vast ocean.
